prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that periodically reads moisture levels from a DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0, an analog resistive sensor, via an MCP3008 analog-to-digital converter connected over the SPI bus. Wire the MCP3008 to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus: chip enable CE0 on GPIO8, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, and SCLK on GPIO11, with the sensor's analog output wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (CH0). Use the pigpio library for all SPI communication with the ADC. Sample the raw 10-bit ADC value, in the range 0-1023, once per second, and log each reading to the console together with a timestamp so the moisture trend can be reviewed later. Implement robust error handling around SPI initialization and every SPI transfer, reporting any failure rather than silently continuing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a graceful shutdown, making sure the SPI handle is closed and pigpio is terminated cleanly on every exit path, including early failures.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads current from an MLX91219 Hall-effect current sensor, which has an analog output, via an ADS1115 analog-to-digital converter over I2C, using the pigpio library for all I2C communication. Wire the ADS1115's ADDR pin to GND, giving it I2C address 0x48 on bus 1; wire the MLX91219's analog output to the ADS1115's AIN0 input; and wire the ADS1115's SDA and SCL lines to the Pi's GPIO2 and GPIO3. Configure the ADS1115 for single-shot mode, AIN0 single-ended (MUX=100), a programmable gain amplifier setting of PGA ±4.096V, and a data rate of 128 samples per second. Every 500ms, log the computed current in amperes to the console, deriving it from the MLX91219's sensitivity of 40mV/A with its zero-current offset centered at mid-supply. Access the ADS1115's 16-bit registers with i2cWriteI2CBlockData and i2cReadI2CBlockData, respecting the correct byte order, and handle I2C write and read errors as well as sensor-absent paths gracefully rather than crashing. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with an AZDelivery KY-026 Flame Sensor Module and an MCP3008 ADC via SPI, using the pigpio library only (do not use wiringPi). Read the KY-026 digital output (D0) on GPIO4 (BCM numbering) and sample its analog output (A0) on MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended); connect the MCP3008 to SPI0 (CE0/GPIO8) at 1 MHz. Approximate ambient temperature from the analog reading using a linear map of the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to 10-40°C. Once per second, log timestamped CSV rows (Timestamp,FlameDetected,Temperature) to flame_data.csv. Implement robust error handling: verify pigpio initialization, SPI open/transfer, and file operations; on sensor-absent or SPI-failure paths, skip the log entry and print a diagnostic. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that monitors two sensors and activates a buzzer when both indicate a fire condition simultaneously, using the pigpio library for all GPIO and I2C access. Connect a Keyes KY-026 Flame Sensor's digital output to GPIO4, using the internal pull-up resistor; the sensor outputs LOW when a flame is detected. Connect an LM393-based Heat Sensor's analog output to an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1 at address 0x48, channel AIN0 (single-ended), configured for single-shot mode, gain ±4.096V, 128 SPS (conversion time ~8.5ms); map the ADC voltage range 0V-3.3V linearly to 20°C-80°C and treat above 60°C as a trigger. Connect the buzzer to GPIO27, active HIGH. Poll the flame sensor and read the temperature every 100ms. Implement a 50ms debounce on the flame sensor using a falling-edge ISR callback, registering a flame event only if at least 50ms have elapsed since the last accepted event. If both a debounced flame event and temperature above 60°C occur together, log the event with a timestamp to fire_log.txt and sound the buzzer for 2 seconds. If only flame is detected, log "Flame detected!"; if only the temperature exceeds 60°C, log the temperature reading. If the ADC read fails (I2C error or sensor absent), log an error and continue without crashing. Check the return values of pigpio initialization, I2C open, the ADC configuration write, the ADC read, and log file creation, printing descriptive errors to stderr for each failure path; on any initialization failure, release all resources acquired so far and exit with code 1. Handle SIGINT by setting a running flag to 0 so the main loop exits cleanly, then turn off the buzzer, deregister the ISR, close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate(). Use only pigpio, never wiringPi or libgpiod; drive the buzzer with a simple digital write rather than PWM; and ensure the code compiles cleanly with gcc -Wall, with no undeclared identifiers or implicit declarations.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to interface with a Melexis MLX91219 current sensor (SOIC8 package, -40°C to 125°C range), which provides an analog output proportional to measured current. Read the analog signal via an external MCP3008 10-bit ADC (VREF = 3.3 V) on SPI0 CE0 (spidev0.0, GPIO8, SPI channel 0) at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0, 8 bits per word, using spidev for SPI access; read single-ended channel 0 with the 3-byte SPI command (0x01, 0x80, 0x00) and extract the 10-bit result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]. Convert the ADC voltage to current using the sensor sensitivity (default 100 mV/A, configurable via -s). If the measured current exceeds a configurable threshold (default 5.0 A, configurable via -t), drive GPIO18 HIGH to turn on a cooling fan; otherwise drive it LOW. Sample once per second and log every reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to current_log.txt. Use libgpiod for all GPIO control, never sysfs or wiringPi, opening the GPIO chip by name (try "gpiochip4" for Pi 5, falling back to chip 0). Implement robust error handling: check every open/ioctl/read/write call, handle SPI transfer failures, and handle sensor-absent conditions where the ADC reads all-zero or all-ones. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM by closing the SPI file descriptor, releasing the GPIO lines, and turning the fan OFF. Include all necessary standard headers, such as stdint.h, so the code compiles cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to interface with an SGX Sensortech / Honeywell MICROceL MICS-4514 CO sensor, a dual-element MOS sensor (NO2 and CO) that outputs raw analog resistance values, using the pigpio library over I2C bus 1 at device address 0x28. Since the Raspberry Pi has no direct analog inputs, read the sensor via an external 16-bit ADC such as an ADS1115 over I2C, or simulate the raw 16-bit ADC readings for the CO element. Every 5 seconds, read the raw 16-bit CO resistance value, convert it to a CO concentration in PPM using a calibrated logarithmic curve, and log the timestamped PPM value to co_log.txt. Implement robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, I2C handle creation, and I2C read failures such as a sensor-absent condition or bus errors. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM. Do not use the deprecated wiringPi library.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to interface with an Adafruit TCS34725 I2C color sensor (I2C address 0x29, bus 1) using the pigpio library for I2C (not wiringPi). Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus, exiting with a non-zero error code if either fails. Verify the sensor is present by reading the ID register (0x12) and checking that the lower 4 bits equal 0x44; exit with an error if the ID does not match. Configure the sensor by setting the integration time (ATIME, register 0x01) to 0xFF (2.4 ms) and the gain (CONTROL, register 0x0F) to 0x01 (4x), then power on and enable the ADC (ENABLE, register 0x00 = 0x01 | 0x02), waiting at least 3 ms after power-on before reading. Every 1 second, read the 16-bit clear, red, green, and blue values from registers 0x14-0x1B and append a line to color_log.csv formatted as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,clear,red,green,blue, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Check every I2C read/write return value; on a transient I2C read failure, print a warning to stderr and continue, and on 3 consecutive failures, exit gracefully. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle, flushes and closes the CSV file, and calls gpioTerminate(), and avoid blocking sleep calls that would prevent signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to read analog values from two Seeed Studio Grove Moisture Sensors. Because the Raspberry Pi has no built-in ADC, connect the sensors to an MCP3008 SPI ADC via the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus (CE0 on GPIO8, MISO on GPIO9, MOSI on GPIO10, SCLK on GPIO11), wiring the two sensors to MCP3008 channels 0 and 1. Use the modern libgpiod API, not sysfs or wiringPi, to control the MCP3008 chip-select line, and standard Linux spidev (/dev/spidev0.0) for SPI communication. Read both channels, map the raw 10-bit ADC values (0-1023) to a 0-100% moisture scale, and log timestamped readings to a CSV file named moisture_log.csv with header Timestamp,Moisture1,Moisture2. Sample every 5 seconds. Implement robust error handling: check all SPI and libgpiod initialization calls, handle sensor-absent or SPI bus-error paths gracefully, and ensure clean release of all resources, including SPI file descriptors and libgpiod lines, on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to interface with a Melexis MLX91211 Triaxis Current Sensor, logging current readings in Amperes to a comma-separated current_log.csv file, and simulating an overcurrent safety system for a DC motor. The MLX91211 is an analog ratiometric Hall-effect sensor, not an SPI device, so read it via an MCP3008 ADC connected over hardware SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8, SCLK on GPIO11, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9), with the sensor's analog output wired to MCP3008 channel 0. Use the modern libgpiod API for GPIO control and spidev for SPI communication with the MCP3008 (not bcm2835 or wiringPi). Sample the sensor every 1 second, convert the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to a voltage (0-3.3V), then to current using a sensitivity of 0.1 V/A and an offset of 0.05V. If the current exceeds 10.0A, drive a motor shutdown pin (GPIO17) LOW to disable the motor, log the event, wait 1 second, then drive it HIGH to re-enable. Check all open(), ioctl(), read(), and file I/O operations for errors, and retry SPI communication errors up to 3 times. Implement signal handling (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown, closing all file descriptors and releasing GPIO lines cleanly on exit. Log each reading as timestamp,current_in_Amperes, writing the header if the file is new or empty.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to interface with a Melexis MLX90817 absolute pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x40, using the pigpio library for I2C. Once per second, read the 16-bit pressure value from register 0x00 and convert it to pressure in kPa using pressure_kPa = (raw_value / 65535.0) * 500.0. Log each reading with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp to a comma-separated file named pressure_log.csv with columns timestamp,pressure_kPa, opening the file once at startup with a header row rather than on every write, and flushing after each write. Check every pigpio/I2C call and file operation for errors; on an I2C read failure, print an error to stderr with the register and the pigpio error code, and continue the loop without logging. Handle sensor-absent scenarios, including I2C open failure or repeated read failures. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to interface with a Melexis MLX90834 pressure sensor. The MLX90834 is a SENT-only MEMS pressure sensor with no native I2C interface, so read its analog pressure output via a generic I2C ADC bridge, an ADS1115 at address 0x48, using the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO. Configure the ADS1115 to read single-ended on AIN0 (pressure signal) and AIN1 (NTC temperature signal) at a gain of 2/3 (FSR ±6.144V), 128 SPS. Convert the ADC voltage to pressure using a linear transfer function (0V = 0 kPa, 5V = 400 kPa) and to temperature using a simplified linear NTC approximation (1V = 0°C, 2V = 100°C). Every 1 second, display the pressure (kPa) and temperature (°C) on the console, and drive a warning LED on GPIO17 (active-high) HIGH when pressure exceeds 105.0 kPa. Implement robust error handling: validate every pigpio call, retry failed I2C reads up to 3 times, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads motor current using a Melexis MLX91209 Hall-effect current sensor (analog output) via an MCP3008 10-bit SPI ADC, using only the pigpio library (no wiringPi). Connect the MLX91209 analog output to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended), with the MCP3008 on SPI0 CE0 (GPIO8 CE, GPIO11 SCLK, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO9 MISO) at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0. The MCP3008 protocol uses a 3-byte transfer: a start bit (0x01), a single-ended channel configuration byte, and a zero pad byte; extract the 10-bit result from the last two bytes of the response. Convert the 10-bit ADC reading to a voltage (0-3.3V full-scale, 1024 steps), then to current using the sensor's zero-current midpoint at Vcc/2 and a sensitivity of 66 mV/A. Sample every 100ms and log each reading with a timestamp to current_log.txt in append mode, flushing after every write. Implement a safety monitor: if current exceeds 10A, assert GPIO27 HIGH to trigger a motor shutdown, log an OVERCURRENT event, and stop the program. Handle all error paths: pigpio initialization failure, SPI open/transfer errors, invalid ADC values, and file I/O errors. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, cleanly close the SPI handle, close the log file, reset GPIO27 to LOW, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with a Honeywell MICROceL MCO-S4 CO sensor whose analog voltage output is read via an external MCP3008 ADC connected to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus (CE0 on BCM GPIO8, SCLK on BCM 11, MOSI on BCM 10, MISO on BCM 9), with the CO sensor's analog output wired to MCP3008 channel 0. Use the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to configure the SPI bus at 1 MHz (SPI mode 0) and to control an alarm on BCM GPIO4. Read the ADC continuously, once per second, convert the 10-bit ADC value to a voltage using a 3.3V reference, and drive the alarm on BCM GPIO4 HIGH if the voltage exceeds 2.5V, or LOW if it is 2.5V or below. Check the return values of gpioInitialise(), spiOpen(), and the SPI transfer function; if an SPI transfer fails, log the error to the log file, ensure the alarm is turned off for safety, and wait 1 second before retrying. Log every valid reading to a file named co_log.txt in the format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,Voltage: X.XX V, one line per reading. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths by handling SIGINT and SIGTERM to close the SPI handle, close the log file, turn off the alarm, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor methane levels with a Honeywell MICROpeL Model 41000-020 Combustible Gas Sensor (analog output) connected to an MCP3008 SPI ADC. Wire the MCP3008 as follows: VDD/VREF to Pi 3.3V (pin 1), DGND/AGND to Pi GND, CLK to GPIO11 (SCLK), DOUT to GPIO9 (MISO), DIN to GPIO10 (MOSI), CS/SHDN to GPIO8 (CE0), with the sensor's analog output feeding MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended). Read the ADC once per second via SPI bus 0, channel 0, at 1 MHz, mode 0, using the MCP3008 3-byte SPI command sequence for single-ended channel 0 (start byte 0x01, config byte 0x80, dummy byte 0x00) and extracting the 10-bit result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]. Convert the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to a methane concentration in PPM using linear scaling (0 -> 0 PPM, 1023 -> 5000 PPM). Log every reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to methane_log.txt in append mode; if the concentration exceeds 1000 PPM, print a visible leak alarm to stderr. Implement robust error handling: check gpioInitialise(), spiOpen(), spiXfer(), fopen(), and localtime_r(); on an SPI transfer failure, log the error to stderr and continue rather than crash. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the SPI handle, terminating pigpio, and closing any open file handle. Do not use wiringPi, and use pigpio's negative-handle error codes directly rather than calling gpioErrno.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read pressure data from a Melexis MLX90830 analog pressure sensor. Since the MLX90830 provides a ratiometric analog output, interface it via an external ADS1115 16-bit ADC at I2C address 0x48 on the Pi's I2C bus 1 (SDA=GPIO2, SCL=GPIO3), with the sensor's analog output connected to the ADS1115's AIN0 channel, using the pigpio library for I2C communication. Read the ADC at 1Hz, convert the raw value to a voltage, then to pressure in kPa using a linear transfer function assuming a 0.5V offset at 0 kPa and a sensitivity of 0.1 V/kPa. Log valid pressure readings in the 0-100 kPa range with ISO-8601 timestamps to pressure_log.txt. Implement robust error handling: check all I2C/ADC initialization and read operations, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and validate the pressure range. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown via SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with a Honeywell HIH-4602-A humidity sensor via SPI using the pigpio library. The HIH-4602-A provides an analog voltage output for relative humidity and contains an integral thermistor for temperature measurement; since the Raspberry Pi lacks analog inputs, use an external 12-bit MCP3208 ADC on SPI0 (CE0/GPIO8) to read both the humidity output and the thermistor voltage. Calculate relative humidity using the sensor's transfer function Vout = 0.824 + 0.0315 * RH with a 5.0V supply, and calculate temperature from the thermistor using a Beta parameter equation with Beta = 3950K and R0 = 10kΩ at 25°C. Trigger an email alert via ssmtp if humidity exceeds 80%. Log readings to humidity_log.txt in comma-separated format (timestamp, humidity, temperature) with robust error handling for pigpio initialization, SPI transfer failures, and file I/O. Implement clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to read temperature data from a TMP36 analog temperature sensor via an external MCP3208 12-bit SPI ADC. Connect the TMP36 signal output to MCP3208 channel 0 (CH0, pin 1), and connect the MCP3208 SPI interface to the Pi 5's SPI0: CE0 (GPIO8), SCLK (GPIO11), MOSI (GPIO10), MISO (GPIO9), with the MCP3208's VDD and VREF tied to 3.3V. Use the modern libgpiod API, not sysfs or wiringPi, to manually control the MCP3208 CS line (GPIO8 on gpiochip4), and use spidev (/dev/spidev0.0) for SPI communication, configured for Mode 0, 8 bits per word, and 1 MHz max speed. Read the ADC at 1Hz, convert the 12-bit value (0-4095) to a voltage using VREF = 3.3V, then to Celsius using Temp = (Voltage - 0.5) / 0.01. Log each reading to a comma-separated temperature_log.csv file formatted as timestamp,temperature_celsius, writing the header only if the file is newly created. Implement robust error handling: check SPI open/ioctl/transfer operations, validate ADC readings, and handle sensor-absent or out-of-range conditions, such as a voltage outside the TMP36's valid range of -40C to 125C. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully close the SPI device, release GPIO lines, and close the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to interface with an Analog Devices ADXL335 analog accelerometer via an MCP3008 10-bit ADC on SPI0, CE0/GPIO8, at 1 MHz, SPI Mode 0, using the pigpio library for SPI and GPIO. Connect the ADXL335 X/Y/Z outputs to MCP3008 channels 0/1/2. At 100 Hz, log the X, Y, Z raw ADC values to impact_log.txt, timestamped and comma-separated. Compute the acceleration magnitude in g using a 3.3V supply, with the ADXL335's 0g point at 1.65V and a sensitivity of 300 mV/g, and flag impacts exceeding 2.0g with an 'IMPACT DETECTED' line in the log. Implement robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, SPI open, every spiXfer return value, and the file open call, and validate that ADC reads are within range. Handle SIGINT cleanly by closing SPI, closing the log file, and calling gpioTerminate. Ensure CS (GPIO8) is managed correctly around each SPI transfer.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to read data from a Silicon Labs Si1172-A30-GMR Optical Heart Rate Sensor using I2C communication via the pigpio library (never wiringPi), on I2C bus 1 at the default 7-bit address 0x49. Log data to a comma-separated file named biometric_log.csv, with a header row, including a Unix timestamp, HR (bpm), SpO2 (%), and an error flag (0 = OK, 1 = read error, 2 = sensor absent/uninitialized). Sample once per second, flushing the file after each write, and handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown by closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the log file. Check the return value of every pigpio I2C call, distinguish between transient I2C errors and a completely absent sensor (an i2cOpen failure), and log an error row with the appropriate error flag when a read fails rather than crashing. Use the Si1172's command-based register access protocol: write the command register (0xC0) to trigger a measurement, then read the FIFO or data registers (0xC1-0xC4) for the raw photoplethysmography samples. Since the Si1172 requires a proprietary algorithm to convert raw PPG samples to HR/SpO2, read the raw 16-bit IR and RED ADC values from the FIFO and log those as proxy values for HR and SpO2 respectively, documenting this limitation in code comments.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to interface with a Honeywell SpiroQuant A+ ES1-005 Mass Flow Sensor for use in a portable oxygen concentrator monitoring system, using the pigpio library (SPI mode 0, 1 MHz baud, SPI channel 0 on CE0/GPIO8). The SpiroQuant A+ outputs an analog signal proportional to flow rate; since the Raspberry Pi lacks an ADC, read it via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI and convert the value to flow rate using a linear scaling formula where 0-3.3V maps to 0-5.0 L/min. Log every 1 second with a microsecond-precision timestamp in the format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.uuuuuu,flow_rate to a comma-separated file named flow_log.csv, flushing after each write to ensure data integrity in a portable device. Implement robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, SPI open, every SPI transfer, and the ADC read; handle sensor-absent conditions, where the ADC returns 0 or full-scale, and SPI bus-error paths. Validate that the flow rate is within the plausible range of 0.0 to 5.0 L/min, logging errors to stderr but continuing to run. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, with SIGINT/SIGTERM handling to close SPI, terminate pigpio, and close the file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to read temperature and pressure data from a TDK ICP-10125 I2C sensor using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open/ioctl/read/write), not wiringPi. The sensor is connected to I2C bus 1 at address 0x67. Log timestamped readings to a comma-separated environmental_data.csv file and display the data on the console for real-time monitoring in a weather station prototype. Use the ICP-10125 measurement command 0x6845 to trigger a high-precision reading, wait for the conversion to finish, then read the 6-byte result (pressure MSB/LSB, temperature MSB/LSB, and CRC bytes). Apply the official ICP-10125 calibration formulas to convert the raw ADC values to temperature in °C and pressure in Pa. Implement robust error handling: check every I2C syscall (open, ioctl, write, read) and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths by logging the error and retrying after 5 seconds. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths by closing the I2C file descriptor and the CSV log file, and use signal handling (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown. Sample every 5 seconds.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that samples audio from two STMicroelectronics MP23ABS1 analog MEMS microphones using the pigpio library. Connect the microphones' analog outputs to an external MCP3008 ADC on the hardware SPI0 bus (CE0, GPIO8). Implement a basic noise-cancellation algorithm by subtracting the two audio streams, and output the resulting audio data to the terminal in CSV format. Implement a simple gain control via command-line arguments. Ensure robust error handling for pigpio initialization, SPI configuration, and sensor-absent/bus-error paths, and handle SIGINT for clean resource release on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to interface with a Vegetronix VH400 soil moisture sensor using the pigpio library for SPI control. Connect the sensor's analog output to channel 0 (CH0) of an MCP3008 10-bit ADC, which communicates with the Pi over SPI0 (CE0). Log the moisture readings to a file named moisture_log.txt as comma-separated values of ISO 8601 UTC timestamps and raw 10-bit ADC readings (0-1023). Sample once every 60 seconds in an infinite loop. Implement robust error handling: check all pigpio initialization and SPI transfer calls, validate the ADC range, and handle file I/O errors gracefully. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM by closing the SPI handle and terminating the pigpio library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read analog voltage values from a Keyes KY-026 Flame Sensor using an MCP3008 ADC via SPI, logging temperature-compensated voltage readings and a flame detection flag to flame_log.txt, and triggering a GPIO-based buzzer on flame detection, using the libgpiod C library (not wiringPi) for both GPIO buzzer control and SPI communication via /dev/spidev0.0. Configure the MCP3008 SPI link in mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0) at 1 MHz with a 3-byte transfer (start bit, single-ended config, dummy byte), extracting the 10-bit ADC value correctly. Connect the KY-026's analog output (AO) to MCP3008 CH0. Drive the buzzer, connected to GPIO18 (BCM), ON continuously while flame is detected and OFF otherwise. Read ambient temperature from a local file, ambient_temp.txt, falling back to 25.0°C if it is missing or invalid. Sample the sensor every 500ms. If the SPI transfer fails, log the error to stderr and the log file, skip the iteration, and turn the buzzer OFF for safety; if the ADC value is out of the 0-1023 range, retry up to 3 times before failing the iteration. Treat a compensated voltage above 1.0V as flame detected, computing it as voltage + (temperature - 25.0) * 0.001. Log each reading in the format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,raw_adc,voltage,compensated_voltage,temperature,flame_detected. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully: stop the loop, turn off the buzzer, close the log file, and release all libgpiod resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with a DFRobot Gravity Analog Water Level Sensor via an MCP3008 10-bit ADC, using the pigpio library for all GPIO and SPI operations (do not use wiringPi). Connect the MCP3008 to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus (CE0 on GPIO8, MISO on GPIO9, MOSI on GPIO10, SCLK on GPIO11), and wire the water level sensor's analog output to MCP3008 channel 0. Initialize pigpio and open SPI channel 0 (CE0) at 1 MHz with SPI mode 0 (flags=0), checking all return codes and aborting gracefully on failure. Every 5 seconds, read the 10-bit ADC value from MCP3008 channel 0 using a 3-byte SPI transfer (start bit 0x01, config byte 0x80|channel<<4, padding 0x00; parse the result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]), convert it to a percentage of the 0-1023 range, and print it to stdout. Log every reading to a JSON file named water_levels.json as a valid JSON array of objects, each containing an ISO 8601 timestamp with milliseconds and the water_level percentage; keep the file valid JSON even if the program is interrupted by opening with a '[' prefix, flushing after each entry, and closing with ']' on shutdown. Turn an LED connected to GPIO17 ON when the water level exceeds 75%, and OFF when it drops below 70% (hysteresis), driving it as a pigpio output. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop the main loop, close the SPI handle, turn off the LED, terminate pigpio, and close the JSON file cleanly. Handle SPI transfer errors (spiXfer returning less than 0) by logging the error via pigpio_error() and skipping that reading without crashing; use pigpio_error() for all pigpio error messages, not gpioErrText, and sleep in small increments (about 100ms via gpioDelay) so signals are handled promptly.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to read airflow data from an analog Honeywell AWM7300V mass airflow sensor via an external MCP3008 10-bit ADC, using the pigpio library. Connect the MCP3008 over SPI0 (CE0 on physical pin 24, SCLK on physical pin 23, MOSI on physical pin 19, MISO on physical pin 21), with the AWM7300V output connected to MCP3008 channel 0. Sample the sensor every 100 milliseconds and log timestamped readings (ISO 8601 format) and converted flow rates in Liters Per Minute (LPM) to a comma-separated file named airflow_log.csv, including a CSV header on startup if the file is newly created. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialization, SPI transmission failures, and file I/O errors. Ensure clean resource release of SPI handles, files, and pigpio on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown via SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to monitor a potted plant using a HiLetgo Soil Moisture Sensor (analog resistive sensor) connected to an MCP3008 ADC, reading it via SPI using the pigpio library (never wiringPi). Wire the MCP3008 on SPI CE0 (bus 0, channel 0) at 500 kHz, single-ended mode, reading ADC channel 0, with the HiLetgo sensor's analog output connected to MCP3008 CH0 and its VCC at 3.3V. Calibrate raw ADC value 300 as 0% moisture (dry air) and 700 as 100% moisture (immersed in water), with lower raw values indicating drier soil. Every 60 seconds, log the timestamp and moisture percentage to plant_data.txt in the format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, <moisture_percent>, appending each entry. If moisture drops below 30%, trigger an email alert via msmtp, piping the email body via popen (not system with shell interpolation), and validate the msmtp exit status. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 (64-bit Bookworm, kernel 6.6+) using libgpiod to detect proximity via a GP2Y0A21YK0F Sharp IR distance sensor whose analog output is read through an ADS1115 ADC at I2C address 0x48 over /dev/i2c-1 using ioctl(I2C_SLAVE) and I2C_RDWR. Wiring: ADS1115 SDA to GPIO2, SCL to GPIO3, ADDR to GND (address 0x48), A0 to the IR sensor's analog output; a 5V relay module's IN line is on GPIO17 (active-high) and simulates a magnetic door lock release, and a magnetic reed door sensor is on GPIO27 (active-low, pulled high, LOW = door open). Use libgpiod for all digital lines. On startup, take 10 baseline samples 50 ms apart and set the trigger threshold to 80% of their average. Poll the ADC every 200 ms; if the distance reading drops below the calibrated threshold, energize the relay for 3 seconds to release the door lock, then de-energize it, then read the reed sensor and log "door opened" if LOW, otherwise "door not opened". Log every event with millisecond timestamps to /var/log/door_events.log. Check every libgpiod call, I2C ioctl, and file open; handle a sensor-absent I2C read failure by logging and continuing. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, de-energize the relay, release all libgpiod lines, close the I2C file descriptor, and exit cleanly. Do not use sysfs or wiringPi.

I have written a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 (64-bit Bookworm, kernel 6.6+) using libgpiod to detect proximity via a GP2Y0A21YK0F Sharp IR distance sensor whose analog output is read through an ADS1115 ADC at I2C address 0x48 over /dev/i2c-1 using ioctl(I2C_SLAVE) and I2C_RDWR. Wiring: ADS1115 SDA to GPIO2, SCL to GPIO3, ADDR to GND (address 0x48), A0 to the IR sensor's analog output; a 5V relay module's IN line is on GPIO17 (active-high) and simulates a magnetic door lock release, and a magnetic reed door sensor is on GPIO27 (active-low, pulled high, LOW = door open). Use libgpiod for all digital lines. On startup, take 10 baseline samples 50 ms apart and set the trigger threshold to 80% of their average. Poll the ADC every 200 ms; if the distance reading drops below the calibrated threshold, energize the relay for 3 seconds to release the door lock, then de-energize it, then read the reed sensor and log "door opened" if LOW, otherwise "door not opened". Log every event with millisecond timestamps to /var/log/door_events.log. Check every libgpiod call, I2C ioctl, and file open; handle a sensor-absent I2C read failure by logging and continuing. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, de-energize the relay, release all libgpiod lines, close the I2C file descriptor, and exit cleanly. Do not use sysfs or wiringPi.

I have written a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 (64-bit Bookworm, kernel 6.6+) using libgpiod to detect proximity via a GP2Y0A21YK0F Sharp IR distance sensor whose analog output is read through an ADS1115 ADC at I2C address 0x48 over /dev/i2c-1 using ioctl(I2C_SLAVE) and I2C_RDWR. Wiring: ADS1115 SDA to GPIO2, SCL to GPIO3, ADDR to GND (address 0x48), A0 to the IR sensor's analog output; a 5V relay module's IN line is on GPIO17 (active-high) and simulates a magnetic door lock release, and a magnetic reed door sensor is on GPIO27 (active-low, pulled high, LOW = door open). Use libgpiod for all digital lines. On startup, take 10 baseline samples 50 ms apart and set the trigger threshold to 80% of their average. Poll the ADC every 200 ms; if the distance reading drops below the calibrated threshold, energize the relay for 3 seconds to release the door lock, then de-energize it, then read the reed sensor and log "door opened" if LOW, otherwise "door not opened". Log every event with millisecond timestamps to /var/log/door_events.log. Check every libgpiod call, I2C ioctl, and file open; handle a sensor-absent I2C read failure by logging and continuing. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, de-energize the relay, release all libgpiod lines, close the I2C file descriptor, and exit cleanly. Do not use sysfs or wiringPi.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to log simultaneous ADC readings from three MCP3008 chips, each reading an analog soil moisture sensor on channel 0 in single-ended mode, into 'soil_moisture_log.csv' in the format timestamp,sensor1,sensor2,sensor3, logging every 5 seconds and writing the CSV header only if the file is newly created. The three MCP3008 chips share SPI0 (MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, SCLK on GPIO11) at 1 MHz, Mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0), with individual chip-select lines CS0 on GPIO8, CS1 on GPIO7, and CS2 on GPIO25. Use libgpiod for manual CS line control and standard Linux spidev for SPI communication; do not use wiringPi. Send the MCP3008 command as the 3-byte transfer [0x01, (0x08|channel)<<4, 0x00] and take the 10-bit result from the lower 2 bits of byte 1 and all 8 bits of byte 2. Check all return values for SPI open/ioctl, libgpiod requests, file operations, and sensor reads; if a sensor read fails, log -1 for that sensor's value. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a graceful shutdown, releasing all resources by closing every open file descriptor and freeing all libgpiod lines and chips before the process exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to control a submersible 12V water pump connected via a relay to GPIO18 (active-high), triggered by a Vegetronix VH400 soil moisture sensor on channel 0 (CH0) of an MCP3008 SPI ADC, with the MCP3008 on SPI0, CE0 on GPIO8, SPI clock 1 MHz, SPI mode 0. The VH400 outputs 0-3V analog, unlike ratiometric resistive sensors, so map the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to a moisture percentage using experimentally determined dry=200 and wet=800 raw bounds, clamped to 0-100%. Log every moisture reading and pump activation/deactivation with timestamps to 'irrigation.log'. If moisture falls below a configurable threshold (default 30%), activate the pump for a configurable duration (default 10 s), then deactivate; check the soil every configurable interval (default 60 s). Accept command-line options -t threshold, -d duration_seconds, and -s sleep_interval. Handle SPI errors gracefully with up to 3 retries per read; if all retries fail, log the error and skip that irrigation cycle without activating the pump. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, shut off the pump, close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly, and ensure the pump is turned off on all exit paths including SPI open failure.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to sample sound levels from an Adafruit MAX4466 electret microphone amplifier connected to channel 0 of an external MCP3008 ADC via SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8, CLK on GPIO11, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9). Sample the ADC every 10 ms, maintaining an exponential moving average (EMA) of the readings, and log a detected peak whenever the raw value exceeds the EMA by a dynamic threshold margin of 20%, writing each peak to /var/log/sound_events.log with an ISO 8601 timestamp and the sampled value. Handle pigpio initialization errors, SPI communication failures, and log file I/O errors, and gracefully shut down on SIGINT/SIGTERM by releasing all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi to monitor the AIN0 analog input channel of a PCF8591 ADC at I2C address 0x48 on bus /dev/i2c-1 in a continuous loop, using libgpiod for any GPIO needs and Linux I2C via i2c-dev for bus communication (not wiringPi). Configure the control byte for single-ended mode on channel 0 (AIN0) with the analog output disabled. Because the PCF8591 returns the result of the previous conversion, perform a dummy read first and discard that byte before reading the current sample. Sample every 100 ms and print each sample value (0-255) to stdout. Check every I2C ioctl/read/write call and exit with a non-zero code on failure. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl-C) cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to monitor a Honeywell SS49E linear Hall-effect sensor. The SS49E is an analog sensor powered from the 3.3 V rail, so sample its voltage output at 1 Hz via an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1 at address 0x48, single-ended channel AIN0. Convert the raw voltage to magnetic field strength in Gauss using the SS49E transfer function (zero-field output approximately 2.5 V, sensitivity approximately 1.4 mV/Gauss, Vcc = 3.3 V), and store the last 10 readings in a circular buffer. If the rolling average of the buffer exceeds a compile-time threshold (e.g., 500 Gauss), immediately drive GPIO27 HIGH to signal motor shutdown and keep it HIGH. Log all readings, threshold events, and errors via syslog. Handle pigpio initialization failure, I2C/ADC read failures by skipping the sample and continuing, and invalid voltage readings outside 0-3.3 V. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, stop the I2C handle, reset GPIO27 to LOW, terminate pigpio, and close syslog. Do not use wiringPi, and do not include MQTT or networking code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read soil moisture from a Vegetronix VH400 sensor whose analog output is connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC via SPI0 CE0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0. Activate a 12V submersible water pump connected to GPIO18 via a relay when the 10-bit ADC reading drops below a threshold of 300, running the pump for 10 seconds per watering cycle, then reading again every 60 seconds. Log timestamps and moisture levels to 'watering_events.txt'. Implement robust SPI communication error handling by validating the channel, checking the spiXfer return value, and detecting stuck or invalid ADC values, plus graceful GPIO initialization failure recovery. Ensure the pump is deactivated immediately on any error or shutdown path, with clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read analog values from a YL-83 rain sensor whose analog output is wired to channel 0 (CH0) of an MCP3008 ADC on SPI0 (CE0, bus 0), with the MCP3008 VDD at 3.3 V so ADC full-scale = 1023, read in single-ended mode. Use SPI mode 0 at 1 MHz. Sample once per second and map the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to a rainfall intensity level of 0-10, where 0 is dry and 10 is heavily raining. Log each reading to stdout with a timestamp, the raw ADC value, and the intensity level. Check pigpio initialization, the SPI open, and every spiXfer call; on SPI transfer failure, print an error and retry on the next cycle rather than continuing with stale data. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown by closing the SPI handle and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the pigpio library to read a potentiometer connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC (SPI0, CE0 on GPIO8) and uses the 10-bit reading to control the duty cycle of a PWM motor on GPIO18. Configure SPI at 1 MHz, mode 0, and PWM at 1 kHz with a range of 0-1023 so the ADC value maps directly to the duty cycle. Continuously read the ADC and update the PWM every 100 ms, printing both values to stdout. Check pigpio initialization, verify the SPI handle, check every SPI transfer result, and handle transient SPI errors without crashing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so the program exits cleanly, stopping PWM and releasing all pigpio resources. Do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a Honeywell SS49E linear Hall-effect sensor. The sensor is analog, powered from 3.3V (zero-gauss output approximately 1.65V, sensitivity approximately 1.0 mV/Gauss = 0.001 V/Gauss), so read it via an ADS1115 ADC on I2C bus 1 at address 0x48, single-ended input on AIN0, gain PGA=4.096V. Output the magnetic field strength in Gauss to the console every 100 ms. If the field exceeds a user-configurable threshold (Gauss, passed via the -t command-line argument, default 100.0), blink an LED on GPIO17 rapidly (50 ms on / 50 ms off) for 1 second. Validate pigpio and I2C initialization, check every I2C read, and handle ADC communication failures gracefully. Ensure clean resource release (LED off, pigpio terminated) on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read soil moisture from an HL-69 analog sensor via an MCP3008 ADC (SPI0, CE0 on GPIO8, physical pin 24, ADC channel 0, SPI clock 1 MHz), with the HL-69 analog output connected to MCP3008 CH0. Control a 5V relay module on GPIO17 (active-high) that switches a water pump: activate the relay when moisture drops below 30%, and deactivate it only when moisture recovers above 35% (hysteresis). Publish moisture readings to MQTT topic 'soil_moisture' every 60 s and accept pump_on/pump_off commands on topic 'pump_control', using paho-mqtt v2 callback signatures. Log via syslog. Include robust error handling for SPI open/transfer failures, GPIO write failures, MQTT connect/subscribe failures, and sensor-absent (out-of-range) conditions. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM: relay off, SPI closed, MQTT disconnected, pigpio terminated.

Check pigpio init, SPI open, every SPI transfer, and the log file open; handle individual sensor read failures by skipping them in the average. Use signal handlers (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown: close the valve (PWM=0), close SPI, close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to read soil moisture levels from a YL-69 sensor connected to channel 0 (CH0) of an MCP3008 ADC, interfaced via SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8) using the pigpio library at 1 MHz in SPI Mode 0. Ensure the SPI command bytes are correctly formatted for the MCP3008 (start bit, single-ended mode, channel 0) and the 10-bit ADC value is extracted correctly; validate the ADC value against the 10-bit range (0-1023) before converting to a moisture percentage. Log readings with timestamps to 'soil_data.txt' every 5 seconds. Handle potential SPI communication errors gracefully with a retry mechanism of up to 5 attempts with exponential backoff; if SPI fails persistently, skip the reading and log an error. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM, ensuring all SPI handles and pigpio resources are released.

Map the distance reading from a single HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (Trig on GPIO23, Echo on GPIO24) to audio frequency from 220 Hz to 880 Hz, and control the volume (PWM duty cycle on GPIO18, PWM0) using a photoresistor (LDR) read via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that logs ambient light and sound levels with timestamps to a file named "environmental_log.txt". Read ambient light from a BH1750 I2C sensor at address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1, and read sound level from a MAX4466 analog microphone connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI using /dev/spidev0.0. Use the standard Linux i2c-dev API for I2C and the standard Linux spidev API for SPI; do not use the wiringPi library. Sample both sensors every 1 second and format each log entry as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Light: [lux], Sound: [raw ADC value]". Handle I2C and SPI errors gracefully, including sensor-absent or bus-error conditions, without crashing. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, terminate gracefully and cleanly release all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor module connected to GPIO 17, using the libgpiod library. Initialize the GPIO line for input with pull-down enabled, then continuously poll the sensor every 1 second. The sensor's digital output is active HIGH when flame is detected (threshold adjustable via an onboard potentiometer) and operates at 3.3 V logic level. Log each timestamped HIGH/LOW reading to "flame_events.log" in CSV format: timestamp, pin, state. When flame is detected, print an alarm message to stdout. Use only the libgpiod API (gpiod_line_*, gpiod_chip_*) — not sysfs, wiringPi, or pigpio. Check every libgpiod call, print error messages to stderr, and exit with a non-zero status on failure. Clean up GPIO resources on normal exit and on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature from a TMP36 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, mode 0, 500 kHz), converts the reading to Celsius, and outputs a proportional voltage via an MCP4725 I2C DAC at address 0x62 on bus 1. Linearly map the temperature range 0C to 50C to a DAC output of 0V to 3.3V. Use the pigpio library for all GPIO, SPI and I2C access. Check every initialization, SPI transfer, I2C write and file operation; handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully with retries and clear error messages. Log each reading — timestamp, raw ADC value, temperature in C, and DAC voltage — to "temperature_log.txt" and also print it to stdout, sampling every 0.5 seconds. On SIGINT, shut down gracefully: close SPI and I2C, close the log file, and terminate pigpio. Do not use wiringPi or other deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads moisture levels from three DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 analog resistive sensors via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (chip select CE0, SPI mode 0, 1 MHz clock), using the pigpio library. Read all three sensors on MCP3008 single-ended channels 0, 1 and 2, and convert each ADC value (0-1023) to a moisture percentage using moisture = (1.0 - (adc_value / 1023.0)) * 100.0, where 0% is dry and 100% is wet. Log timestamped readings ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "soil_data.txt" in append mode, one line per sensor per cycle, with a 60-second sleep interval between cycles. If spiOpen or spiXfer fails, print an error message and exit with code 1; if a sensor read produces an invalid ADC value, print an error and continue. On SIGINT, close SPI, close the log file, terminate pigpio, and print a goodbye message, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths. Use only pigpio functions (spiOpen, spiXfer, spiClose, gpioInitialise, gpioTerminate, gpioDelay) — do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to sequentially activate and deactivate four Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relays connected to BCM GPIO pins 17, 22, 23 and 24, simulating a basic light sequencer. Use libgpiod calls (gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) with error checking on every call. Initially set all relay pins inactive (LOW, assuming active-high relay modules). In a loop, activate each relay in sequence for 1 second, then deactivate it, with a 1-second delay between relays, repeating the full cycle indefinitely until interrupted. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that deactivates all relays and releases all GPIO lines before exiting. Include no SPI, ADC, temperature-sensor, or logging functionality — the task is relay sequencing only. Use only standard C libraries and libgpiod, not wiringPi or pigpio, and include clear comments explaining each step.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read a Keyes KY-038 sound sensor's analog output through an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (chip select CE0 on GPIO8, mode 0, 1 MHz clock), reading MCP3008 channel 0. When the sound level exceeds a threshold of 500 (10-bit ADC value), turn on an LED connected to GPIO16, log the timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "sound_events.log", and keep the LED on for 500 ms. Read the ADC every 10 ms in the main loop, applying a debounce delay after each trigger. Handle SPI transfer failures, invalid ADC channel selection, and GPIO initialization errors gracefully, checking every pigpio call and file operation. Install a signal handler for SIGINT to cleanly release resources on exit: close SPI, terminate pigpio, and turn off the LED. Use the pigpio library, not wiringPi.

Wire the motor driver as IN1=GPIO17, IN2=GPIO18, ENA=GPIO27 with PWM (range 255, duty 150). Read the rain sensor with the standard 3-byte MCP3008 single-ended transfer: tx[0]=0x01, tx[1]=(0x08|channel)<<4, tx[2]=0x00, parsing the 10-bit result from the low 2 bits of rx[1] and all of rx[2]. Convert the ADC value (0-1023) to a rain level (0-10) so that ADC 1023 maps to rain level 0 (dry) and ADC 0 maps to rain level 10 (heaviest rain), since the sensor outputs higher voltage when dry. Poll every 1 second, and log each timestamped rain reading to "rain_log.txt" in append mode, flushing after every write. When the rain level is at or above a threshold of 5, close the window by driving the motor forward (IN1=1, IN2=0, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds; when it drops below the threshold, open the window by driving the motor in reverse (IN1=0, IN2=1, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds. The window starts in the open state. Handle pigpio initialization failures, SPI open failures, and log file open failures with clear error messages and proper cleanup, checking every init, syscall and I/O return value, and handling SPI transfer and log write failures without crashing. Install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag for graceful shutdown: stop the motor, close SPI, close the log file, and terminate pigpio, releasing all resources on every exit path. Use only the pigpio library, not wiringPi; the program should compile with gcc -o rain rain.c -lpigpio -lrt -lpthread.

When the signal exceeds a threshold of approximately 0.7 x 3.3 V = 2.31 V, corresponding to a raw 10-bit ADC reading of about 700 out of 1023, turn on an LED on GPIO16 for 500 ms, print a timestamped detection message to the console, and apply a 50 ms debounce to avoid false triggers. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads distance from a Sharp GP2Y0A21YK0F IR distance sensor using the sysfs GPIO interface on GPIO 17. Because the sensor's real output is analog and this exercise has no ADC available, treat GPIO 17 as a digital input reading 0 or 1, convert that to a placeholder voltage (0V for low, 3.3V for high), and then convert the voltage to distance using distance (mm) = A / voltage + B, with A = 26.0 and B = -6.0. Log each reading with a timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "distance_log.txt" in append mode. Implement a proximity-based pet feeder activation: if the computed distance is below 200 mm, print "Feeder Activated" to the console; otherwise print "Feeder Idle". Handle GPIO file open or read errors gracefully by printing an error and retrying after 1 second. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, unexport GPIO 17 and exit cleanly. The program should run continuously until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library, together with the standard Linux spidev SPI interface, to read analog soil moisture data from a Vegetronix VH400 sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, SCLK=GPIO11, MOSI=GPIO10, MISO=GPIO9), configured for single-ended mode on channel 0. Using calibrated ADC values of dry=800 and wet=300, if the moisture level drops below 30%, activate a 12V submersible water pump connected to GPIO17 through an active-high relay. Log each reading to "soil_moisture.log" with a timestamp, the moisture percentage, and the pump status (ON/OFF), sampling every 60 seconds continuously. Check every initialization step (libgpiod, SPI, log file), handle sensor read failures gracefully, and validate ADC values. On SIGINT, shut down gracefully by turning off the pump, closing the log file, and releasing all GPIO resources. Use only libgpiod and the standard Linux spidev SPI interface — do not use bcm2835 or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads analog voltage from a DRV5055-A1 Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI, using the Linux spidev interface on /dev/spidev0.0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0, 8 bits per word, together with libgpiod (gpiochip0, line 8) to manually drive chip-select low during each SPI transfer and high afterward. Hardware wiring: MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 3.3 V rail; MCP3008 DOUT to GPIO 10, DIN to GPIO 9, CLK to GPIO 11, and CS/SHDN to GPIO 8; DRV5055-A1 VOUT to MCP3008 channel 0, DRV5055 VCC to 3.3 V. The MCP3008 is a 10-bit ADC (0-1023) with VREF = 3.3 V, so compute Vout_mV = adc_value * 3300 / 1023. The DRV5055-A1 has a sensitivity of 100 mV/mT and a quiescent output of VCC/2 = 1650 mV, so compute the magnetic field B (mT) = (Vout_mV - 1650) / 100. Sample every 500 ms and append a CSV row to "magnetic_log.txt" as <unix_epoch>,<B_mt_two_decimals>. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly, releasing the GPIO line, closing the gpiochip, closing the SPI file descriptor, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library that reads analog voltage from a TI DRV5055VA Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO 8, 9, 10, 11), with the sensor output wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended) and the sensor powered at 3.3 V. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to periodically read analog moisture levels from a YL-69 soil moisture sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI channel 0, CE0, at a 1 MHz baud rate, with the sensor on MCP3008 single-ended channel 0. Use the SPI command format: start bit 0x01, then a single-ended-plus-channel-select byte 0x80 | (channel << 4), then a dummy byte 0x00, reading the 10-bit ADC value as ((rx_buf[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx_buf[2]. prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi to capture a single 1920x1080 JPEG image from a USB camera at /dev/video0 and save it to "image.jpg", using the V4L2 API with memory-mapped (MMAP) buffers. Open the device in blocking mode (O_RDWR without O_NONBLOCK) so VIDIOC_DQBUF blocks until a frame is ready. Query device capabilities and verify V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE and V4L2_CAP_STREAMING are supported. Request the format V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG at 1920x1080 with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, request 4 MMAP buffers, and query, mmap, and queue each one. Start streaming, dequeue one frame, verify buf.bytesused > 0, and write the raw MJPEG bytes directly to disk with no re-encoding. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths: stop streaming, munmap all mapped buffers, free the buffer array, close the file, and close the device fd. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly tears down streaming and releases resources. Check every ioctl, open, mmap, and fopen return value, printing a descriptive error via perror/errno on failure. Do not use any external image libraries.

Write a C program using the libgpiod library to control a camera pan-tilt system with two hobby servos on a Raspberry Pi: the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 and the tilt servo to GPIO5. Four push-buttons, wired active-low with internal pull-ups enabled, control movement: GPIO6 moves tilt up, GPIO7 moves tilt down, GPIO8 moves pan left, and GPIO9 moves pan right. Generate software PWM through libgpiod with a 50 Hz period (20 ms) and pulse widths between 1 and 2 ms, expressed as duty values of 50 to 100 out of 1000. Start both the pan and tilt servos at the mid-position value of 75. Each button press increments or decrements the corresponding servo's position by 5 units, clamped to the range [25, 125], polling all four buttons every 50 ms. Check the return value of every libgpiod call, handling chip-open and line-request failures, and cleanly release all GPIO resources when SIGINT is received.

For autofocus support, query the V4L2_CID_FOCUS_AUTO control via VIDIOC_QUERYCTRL. Check every ioctl return value, and handle the cases where the device node does not exist or cannot be opened, where the camera does not support frame-size or interval enumeration, and where the focus control is not present. Print a clear summary to stdout and exit with a non-zero code on fatal errors.

Write a C program using the pigpio library to control a camera pan-tilt system with two standard hobby servos on a Raspberry Pi: pan servo on GPIO4, tilt servo on GPIO5. Four push-buttons, active-low and wired to ground with internal pull-ups enabled, control movement: UP on GPIO6, DOWN on GPIO7, LEFT on GPIO8, RIGHT on GPIO9. Servos expect a 50 Hz PWM signal with pulse widths between 1000 microseconds and 2000 microseconds; initialize both servos to the center position of 1500 microseconds. While a button is held, increment or decrement the corresponding servo position by 10 microseconds per loop iteration (50 ms loop delay), clamped to the 1000-2000 microsecond range. Initialize the pigpio library and check its return value, printing an error and exiting if it fails. Configure internal pull-up resistors on all button pins, and use gpioServo() for PWM output. Use only pigpio — not wiringPi.

Open /dev/video0 read/write and verify it is a V4L2 video capture device via VIDIOC_QUERYCAP. Check every syscall, ioctl, mmap, fopen, and fwrite return value, printing errno via perror on failure and exiting with EXIT_FAILURE.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that displays real-time CPU temperature, read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, and CPU usage percentage, computed from /proc/stat, on a 128x64 I2C OLED screen using the SSD1306 driver. Use the pigpio library for I2C communication on bus 1, addressing the SSD1306 at 0x3C. Implement a basic 5x7 bitmap font to render the temperature and usage text on the display, updating the display once per second. Handle file read errors by returning specific error strings to the display instead of the missing values, and handle I2C communication failures by logging a message to stderr and exiting gracefully, checking every I2C write operation for an error return. Include signal handling for SIGINT so that all resources are released cleanly on exit.

prompt: Write a C program using the libgpiod library for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix. The matrix rows are anodes, connected via GPIO to +3.3V, and columns are cathodes, connected via GPIO to ground: rows on GPIO17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM numbering), columns on GPIO5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20. Implement a scanning display function that lights one row at a time — row HIGH and column LOW lights an LED (common-anode logic) — using a scan delay of 800 microseconds per row. Create two wave patterns, left-to-right and right-to-left, that shift each frame. Check all libgpiod calls, printing descriptive error messages to stderr and exiting with a non-zero code on failure. Handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing GPIO lines and cleaning up. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated library.

Write a C program using the libgpiod v2 API (gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix with 8 row anodes and 8 column cathodes. Wire row pins GPIO2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 to the row anodes, and column pins GPIO14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 to the column cathodes through current-limiting resistors (e.g. 220 ohm). Scan columns from left to right with a 150 ms delay between columns: for each column, set the corresponding column cathode LOW and all row anodes HIGH to light the entire column, clearing the matrix before each column by setting all column cathodes HIGH and all row anodes LOW. Run the animation indefinitely until interrupted (Ctrl+C). Check every GPIO operation, handling chip-open failure, and cleanly release all GPIO lines on exit using a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an STMicroelectronics VL53L3CX Time-of-Flight multi-target sensor via I2C using the pigpio library. The sensor is connected to I2C bus 1 at the default address 0x29. Initialize the sensor, verifying the sensor model ID during initialization, and periodically read distance measurements for all detected targets, logging the data with an ISO-8601 timestamp to the console every 100 ms. Note that the VL53L3CX requires a complex proprietary initialization sequence; use the standard ST Ultra Lite Driver (ULD) API registers and flow, or clearly stub the proprietary firmware download with a descriptive comment, while fully implementing the I2C communication, error handling, and application logic. Check every I2C read/write return code, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown via SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to interface with a Melexis MLX75031 Time-of-Flight sensor via I2C using the pigpio library. Use I2C bus 1 and the sensor's default address 0x4C. Read the 16-bit distance register at address 0x0D by first writing the register address, then reading two bytes in big-endian order. Log timestamped distance readings to a comma-separated file named "depth_log.csv", writing a CSV header row if the file is newly created, sampling every 100 milliseconds. Include robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, I2C open, I2C read/write operations, and file operations. If an I2C read fails, log an error row with the distance field set to -1 and attempt to re-open the I2C handle. Handle SIGINT for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and log file and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read proximity and ambient light data over I2C (bus 1) from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor at address 0x60. Verify the PART ID register (0x00) reads 0x45, then initialize the sensor by writing to the command register (0x18) to set measurement rates and clear any stale IRQ, handling I2C read failures gracefully. Log readings with ISO-8601 timestamps to "biometric_log.txt", sampling every 500 ms. If the sensor is absent or initialization fails, print a diagnostic to stderr and exit non-zero; if a read fails mid-loop, log the error and continue. Install a SIGINT handler to cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to interface with an E18-D50NK IR proximity sensor via GPIO using the libgpiod library. The E18-D50NK outputs LOW when an object is detected within its calibrated range of 10-30 cm, and HIGH otherwise. Use GPIO line 4 (physical pin 7) for the sensor input and GPIO line 17 (physical pin 11) for an LED output, polling every 100 ms. When an object is detected (sensor reads LOW), blink the LED for 100 ms (ON then OFF) and log a timestamped event to "proximity.log" in ISO 8601 UTC format, e.g. "2024-01-15T12:34:56Z Object detected" — log only on the falling edge (HIGH to LOW transition, object entering range) to avoid duplicate entries while the object remains in range. Open the GPIO chip by name "gpiochip4" (the Raspberry Pi 5 default); if that fails, fall back to gpiod_chip_open_by_name("gpiochip0") — do not use gpiod_chip_open_lookup without arguments. Check all libgpiod calls and handle file I/O errors, ensuring clean resource release — releasing GPIO lines and closing the chip — on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Verify the sensor is present by reading the model ID register 0xC0 and confirming it equals 0xEE; if the read fails or the ID mismatches, print an error and exit cleanly. Perform a single-shot ranging loop: write 0x01 to SYSRANGE_START (register 0x00) to begin a measurement, poll RESULT_INTERRUPT_STATUS (register 0x13) until bit 0 is set, with a timeout of about 100 ms, then read the 16-bit distance from RESULT_RANGE_STATUS (register 0x14, two bytes, little-endian) and clear the interrupt by writing 0x01 to SYSTEM_INTERRUPT_CLEAR (register 0x0B). Print each reading to stdout as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS Distance: <N> mm' every 500 ms. On any I2C read/write error during the loop, print a warning to stderr and continue to the next iteration rather than crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by closing the I2C handle, calling gpioTerminate(), and exiting.

Initialize the sensor by writing 0x01 to the CONFIG register (0x18) to enable proximity mode, then poll bit 0 of the IRQ status register (0x25) to detect data-ready before reading the 16-bit proximity result from registers 0x2A (LSB) and 0x2B (MSB), printing the value every 500 ms. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C cleanly closes the I2C handle and calls gpioTerminate().

When an obstacle is detected, activate a buzzer on GPIO 18 (active-high); when the obstacle is removed, deactivate the buzzer. Poll the sensor every 100 ms and log every state transition with an ISO 8601 timestamp to 'obstacle_log.txt'. Check all libgpiod return values and handle errors robustly, including chip open failure, line request failure, and read/write errors. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all GPIO lines and closing the chip.
raw:
```
$ ./obstacle_detector
```

Initialize pigpio and check for failure, configure trigger as output and echo as input, and measure distance by sending a 10 microsecond trigger pulse and timing the echo pulse width using a speed of sound of 343 m/s. Handle sensor timeouts -- echo stuck low or high for more than 50 ms -- by returning a sentinel error value and skipping that reading. Map valid distances from 2 to 400 cm to servo angle so that 2 cm maps to -90 degrees and 400 cm maps to +90 degrees. Log each reading with a timestamp to sensor_data.log, appending, once every 200 ms until interrupted. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers for graceful shutdown that stop the servo (pulse 0), release resources, and call gpioTerminate() on all exit paths, including when the main loop exits due to a signal, ensuring no GPIO operations occur after termination. Use only valid BCM GPIO numbers on the Pi 4, and do not use GPIO 28.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to interface with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Verify the sensor model ID equals 0xEA at register 0x010F during initialization, perform a software reset by writing 0x00 then 0x01 to register 0x0000, configure the sensor for a 50 ms timing budget, and start ranging by writing 0x01 to register 0x0080. Every 50 ms, poll the data-ready bit (bit 0 of register 0x0089) before reading the 16-bit distance from registers 0x0096-0x0097, and activate a buzzer connected to GPIO23 if the measured distance falls below 100mm. Handle all I2C read/write errors gracefully, with robust error handling for I2C communication failures and sensor absence. Log distance readings using a POSIX message queue. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, message queue, GPIO, and pigpio on SIGINT. Structure the initialization sequence so that the model-ID check, the software reset, and the timing-budget configuration all complete successfully before ranging begins, and treat a failure at any of these steps as a fatal startup error.

Send a 10 microsecond HIGH trigger pulse and use gpioSetAlertFuncEx for interrupt-driven measurement of the echo pulse width, computing distance using a speed of sound of 34300 cm/s divided by 2 for the round trip, and handling pigpio's 32-bit tick wraparound correctly. Valid readings range from 2 cm to 400 cm. Display the distance in centimeters on the console every 100 ms. Activate the buzzer continuously while the distance is less than 30 cm, and turn it off once the distance returns to 30 cm or above. Check pigpio initialization, GPIO mode configuration, and alert registration for errors, and detect and clearly report sensor-absent (timeout/no echo) and invalid reading (out-of-range) conditions. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to control a gate with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x29 and an SG90 servo motor on GPIO18 (BCM, hardware PWM). Automatically open the gate when an object is detected within 20 cm and close it when the path is clear. Implement full bare-metal I2C initialization for the VL53L1X: software reset, wait for boot, start ranging, and read the 16-bit distance. Log all gate events with timestamps to 'gate_log.txt'. Handle I2C communication errors and sensor-absent paths gracefully, with retries. Support remote control using the paho-mqtt v2 callback API, handling force_open, force_close, and status_request commands. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths via signal handling.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor: TRIG on GPIO 23 (physical pin 16, BCM, output, initially LOW) and ECHO on GPIO 24 (physical pin 18, BCM, input with a pull-down resistor). Initialize pigpio with full error checking, printing a diagnostic and exiting non-zero on failure. Generate a 10 microsecond trigger pulse to start each measurement cycle, and register an alert callback on ECHO that captures both rising and falling edge timestamps as pigpio tick values in microseconds. Compute pulse duration as (falling_tick - rising_edge_tick), accounting for pigpio's 32-bit tick wraparound every roughly 72 minutes, and calculate distance using a speed of sound of 343 m/s (0.0343 cm/us), dividing by 2 for the round trip. Validate the pulse width: reject readings below 100 microseconds as noise or above 30000 microseconds as a timeout/no object detected, logging rejected readings as warnings. Log valid readings with an ISO 8601 timestamp to both stdout and an append-mode file named 'distance_log.txt', flushing after each write. Measure every 200 ms (5 Hz); if no valid echo is received within 60 ms of triggering, log a timeout warning and continue. Note in a comment that the HC-SR04's ECHO output is 5V, exceeding the Pi's 3.3V GPIO tolerance, and assume a voltage divider or logic-level converter is present on the ECHO line. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown: close the log file, release GPIO resources via gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) for all GPIO, PWM, and I2C operations to implement a smart parking gate with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/SDA, GPIO3/SCL) at address 0x29 and a servo motor gate actuator. Connect the VL53L1X shutdown pin to GPIO23 (BCM) and its interrupt pin to GPIO24 (BCM); generate the servo PWM signal on GPIO18 (BCM, hardware PWM). Open the gate when an object is detected within 50 cm and close it when the distance exceeds 60 cm, applying hysteresis. Log all gate state changes with timestamps and distances to 'parking_log.txt'. Verify the sensor model ID during initialization, check all I2C read/write operations, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers.
raw:

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to synthesize a theremin-like instrument on a piezo buzzer connected to GPIO18 (PWM0), with pitch controlled by distance read from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24). Set trigger low initially, send a 10 us high pulse, and measure the echo pulse width with microsecond precision using gpioDelay for timing and pull-down resistors on the echo pin; treat a pulse over 100 ms as a timeout, report the error, and reuse the last valid distance. The sensor's full range is 2 cm to 400 cm, but map the practical range of 5 cm to 50 cm linearly to a PWM frequency between 200 Hz and 2000 Hz using frequency = MIN_FREQ + (MAX_FREQ - MIN_FREQ) * (MAX_DIST - distance) / (MAX_DIST - MIN_DIST), clamped to that range, driven through pigpio's gpioHardwarePWM (not sysfs PWM) so the tone changes smoothly and continuously. Check pigpio initialisation and confirm GPIO modes are set correctly, handling sensor read failures gracefully. Print distance and frequency to the console each loop iteration, with a 10 ms delay between readings. Install a SIGINT handler that stops the PWM output and terminates pigpio cleanly.
raw:
```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define TRIGGER_PIN 23
#define ECHO_PIN 24
#define MIN_FREQ 200
#define MAX_FREQ 2000
#define MIN_DIST 5
#define MAX_DIST 50

static volatile int running = 1;

void handler(int signum)
{
    running = 0;
}

int main(void)
{
    int trigger_gpio, echo_gpio, frequency, distance;
    unsigned int start_time, end_time;
    float duration;

    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "pigpio initialisation failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    if (gpioSetMode(TRIGGER_PIN, PI_OUTPUT) < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "gpioSetMode failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    if (gpioSetMode(ECHO_PIN, PI_INPUT) < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "gpioSetMode failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    if (gpioSetPullUpDown(ECHO_PIN, PI_PUD_DOWN) < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "gpioSetPullUpDown failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    if (gpioSetAlertFunc(ECHO_PIN, handler) < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "gpioSetAlertFunc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    trigger_gpio = TRIGGER_PIN;
    echo_gpio = ECHO_PIN;

    signal(SIGINT, handler);

    while (running)
    {
        gpioWrite(trigger_gpio, 0);
        gpioDelay(10);
        gpioWrite(trigger_gpio, 1);
        gpioDelay(10);
        gpioWrite(trigger_gpio, 0);

        start_time = gpioTick();
        while (gpioRead(echo_gpio) == 0)
        {
            if (gpioTick() - start_time > 100000)
            {
                fprintf(stderr, "timeout\n");
                return 1;
            }
        }

        end_time = gpioTick();
        duration = (float)(end_time - start_time) / 1000000.0;
        distance = (int)(duration * 34000.0 / 2.0);

        if (distance < MIN_DIST)
        {
            distance = MIN_DIST;
        }
        else if (distance > MAX_DIST)
        {
            distance = MAX_DIST;
        }

        frequency = MIN_FREQ + (MAX_FREQ - MIN_FREQ) * (MAX_DIST - distance) / (MAX_DIST - MIN_DIST);

        gpioHardwarePWM(echo_gpio, frequency, 1000000);

        printf("distance: %d, frequency: %d\n", distance, frequency);
        gpioDelay(10000);
    }

    gpioHardwarePWM(echo_gpio, 0, 0);
    gpioTerminate();

    return 0;
}

Initialise the sensor by writing 0x01 to register 0x01 (continuous measurement mode), 0x00 to register 0x02 (5 m range), and 0x01 to register 0x00 to trigger a measurement; read the distance from registers 0x0C (low byte) and 0x0D (high byte) using spiXfer, since pigpio has no spiWriteRead function. Continuously read distance in millimeters (range 200-5000 mm) with a 100 ms delay between readings, and log each reading with a timestamp to 'distance_log.csv' opened in append mode, closed properly on exit. Handle SPI communication errors, sensor initialisation failures, and sensor-absent conditions gracefully, logging errors to stderr and continuing to run indefinitely. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the SPI handle, release resources, and flush the log file.
code:
