prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the standard Linux I2C ioctl interface (no third-party C libraries) to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1175 ambient light and proximity sensor at its default I2C address 0x60. Read the 16-bit visible ambient light value from registers 0x22 (low byte) and 0x23 (high byte) every 5 seconds. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a CSV file named 'proximity_log.csv' with the header row 'timestamp,als_visible'. Check every I2C open/read/write call for errors, handling both sensor-absent conditions and bus-error paths without terminating unexpectedly, and cleanly release the I2C file descriptor and the log file on all exit paths, including those triggered by SIGINT and SIGTERM. Include <stdint.h> for the uint8_t and uint16_t types used to hold the register bytes and the combined light reading.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read ambient light (ALS) and proximity (PS1) data from a Silicon Labs Si1120 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x60. Reset the sensor by writing 0x01 to register 0x30, then verify the part ID at register 0x00 equals 0x41. Read ALS data from registers 0x22 (low byte) and 0x23 (high byte) and proximity data from registers 0x18 (low byte) and 0x19 (high byte), combining each pair into a 16-bit little-endian value. Sample every 500 ms until SIGINT (Ctrl+C) is received, logging each reading together with a timestamp in YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS format to 'si1120_log.txt', which the program opens in append mode so earlier readings are preserved across runs. Retry I2C operations up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between attempts before giving up on that reading, check the return value of every initialisation call and syscall, print descriptive errors to stderr so a failure can be diagnosed, and release all resources (I2C handle, log file, pigpio) on any failure path as well as on normal exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses standard Linux I2C ioctl calls (open, ioctl, read, write) on /dev/i2c-1 to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1182-A-GM optical sensor at I2C address 0x39. Initialise the sensor by verifying the part ID register (0x00) and configuring the measurement rate register (0x08) to 0x07. Every 100 ms, read ambient light data from registers 0x22-0x23 and proximity data from registers 0x24-0x25, each as a 16-bit little-endian value; convert ambient light to lux using lux = raw * 0.1, and log proximity as the raw value with no conversion. Log each timestamped reading (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm) to 'biometric_log.txt' in CSV format as timestamp,lux,proximity, and print the same reading to stdout. Check every I2C read/write operation for errors, handle sensor absence (a failed part ID read) gracefully, and report I2C bus errors such as NACK with appropriate messages. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the I2C file descriptor and log file, and ensure all resources are released on every exit path, including error exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library's I2C functions (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cWriteByteData, i2cReadByteData, i2cClose, gpioTerminate) to continuously read proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor at I2C address 0x60. Initialise the sensor with the following write sequence: 0x03 to register 0x07 (hardware key), 0x02 to register 0x06 (MEAS_RATE, 2 ms), 0x00 to register 0x1A (no interrupt), 0x0B to register 0x21 (ALS_VIS_IR_ADC_COUNTER), 0x00 to register 0x24 (ALS_VIS_ADC_GAIN), 0x49 to register 0x22 (PS_ADC_COUNTER, 16-bit, 1/15 gain), 0x03 to register 0x0C (PS_LED21, 180 mA), 0x0F to register 0x0F (PS_LED3, 180 mA), 0x03 to register 0x11 (PS_ADC_MISC, small IR), 0x07 to register 0x0D (PS_ADC_GAIN, 7.7x), and 0x03 to register 0x80 (COMMAND, PS_FORCE). After initialisation, continuously read the proximity value from registers 0x16 (PS1_DATA0, low byte) and 0x17 (PS1_DATA1, high byte), combining them into a 16-bit unsigned integer, and append each reading with a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) to 'proximity_log.txt'. Check every I2C write/read operation for errors; on a communication failure, log the error together with a timestamp and retry up to 3 times before exiting, and handle sensor initialisation failures by reporting a clear, specific error message rather than failing silently. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates pigpio. The program should run indefinitely, taking one reading per cycle, until it is interrupted by the user.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an interrupt-driven HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO17, echo on GPIO18) and activate a buzzer on GPIO27 when the distance falls below 20 cm. Configure the trigger pin as output, the echo pin as input with a falling/rising edge alert callback, and the buzzer pin as output. Generate a 10 us trigger pulse on GPIO17, then measure the echo pulse width using an interrupt handler that records the rising and falling edge timestamps, computing distance in cm as round-trip time * 0.0343 / 2 (speed of sound = 0.0343 cm/us). Print the distance to stdout every second; if the distance is below 20 cm set the buzzer pin high, otherwise set it low. Initialise pigpio and check for errors, exiting with a clear message if initialisation fails; check all pigpio calls (gpioSetMode, gpioSetAlertFuncEx, gpioWrite, gpioDelay) and print errors to stderr if they fail. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by terminating pigpio and exiting, with proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

After writing the register address to read, wait 10 ms for conversion, then read the temperature register (0x01) and the humidity register (0x02). Convert readings using T = (175.72 * raw) / 65536.0 - 46.85 and H = (125.0 * raw) / 65536.0 - 6.0. Verify pigpio initialisation, the I2C bus open, and every I2C read/write operation; if a transaction fails, close and re-open the I2C handle to attempt recovery. Initialise pigpio and verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (expect 0x68). Reset the device via PWR_MGMT_1 (0x6B), wait for it to stabilize, then clear the sleep bit. Handle I2C read/write errors and sensor-absent conditions without terminating the loop unexpectedly. Poll the sensor every 1 second, and log the ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, differential pressure in Pa, and temperature in °C to a comma-separated file named 'pressure_log.csv', writing a header row if the file is new. Check all pigpio and file I/O operations, validate the CRC-8 checksum for every reading (polynomial 0x31, initialization 0xFF), and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses standard Linux I2C ioctls on /dev/i2c-1 to interface with a Sensirion SHT40 humidity and temperature sensor on I2C bus 1 (SDA on GPIO2, SCL on GPIO3) at the 7-bit address 0x44, simulating a smart greenhouse environment monitor. Use the high-repeatability measurement command 0xFD, which returns 6 bytes: 2 bytes temperature MSB+LSB, 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes humidity MSB+LSB, 1 CRC byte; wait at least 10 ms for the measurement to complete before reading. Validate every reading with the Sensirion CRC-8 algorithm (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF). Log temperature and humidity readings with timestamps to 'sht40_log.txt' every 5 seconds. Robustly handle I2C open, ioctl, write, and read errors; if the sensor is absent or a read fails, log an error and retry on the next cycle. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a Silicon Labs Si7015 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40. Use the Si7015's No Hold Master mode: write command 0xF3 for temperature or 0xF5 for humidity, then poll-read two bytes until the measurement is ready (up to about 20 ms per measurement). Convert raw values using Temperature = (175.72 * raw / 65536.0) - 46.85 and Humidity = (125.0 * raw / 65536.0) - 6.0, clamping humidity to 0-100 %RH. Log each reading with a timestamp to 'sensor_data.txt' in append mode and also print it to the console, sampling every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialisation, I2C open, every I2C write/read, and file open; retry on transient I2C failures and exit cleanly on sensor-absent or bus-error conditions, using pigpio_error() (which returns a const char*) and <errno.h>'s strerror() for diagnostics. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing any open file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the Linux I2C character-device API (<linux/i2c-dev.h>, open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor on /dev/i2c-1 at address 0x25, for a ventilation system monitoring application. Trigger continuous measurement with command 0x362F, wait approximately 45 ms, then read 9 bytes: 3 bytes pressure + CRC, 3 bytes temperature + CRC, and 3 bytes scale factor + CRC, validating the CRC-8 checksum for each word. Convert raw pressure to Pa by dividing by its scale factor, and raw temperature to °C as raw/200 - 45. Log the timestamp, pressure in Pa, and temperature in °C, comma-separated, to 'airflow_data.txt' every 100 ms, including a header row. Check every syscall for errors, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths without crashing, and validate every CRC before using the corresponding value. Cleanly release all resources, including the I2C file descriptor and the log file, on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to sample temperature from a Sensirion STS30-DIS temperature-only sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x4A. Every 5 seconds, issue the single-shot high-repeatability measurement command 0x2C06, wait at least 15 ms for conversion, then read 3 bytes (2 data bytes plus 1 CRC byte) and validate the CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial 0xFF). Convert the raw value to degrees Celsius using T = -45 + 175 * (raw / 65535). Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'enclosure_temp_log.txt'. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, including initialisation, write, read, and CRC mismatch, logging any errors with timestamps to 'error_log.txt'. Handle SIGINT for a graceful shutdown, closing all handles and releasing resources cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open(), ioctl(), read(), write() on /dev/i2c-1) to interface with a Sensirion SHT40 humidity and temperature sensor at its fixed address 0x44, simulating a smart greenhouse environment monitor. Use the high-repeatability measurement command 0xFD, which returns 6 bytes: [T_MSB, T_LSB, T_CRC, RH_MSB, RH_LSB, RH_CRC]; wait at least 8.5 ms after issuing the command before reading. Convert raw temperature using T = -45 + 175 * raw/65535 and humidity using RH = 100 * raw/65535, validating every read with the Sensirion CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, init 0xFF). Log timestamped temperature and humidity readings to 'sht40_log.txt' every 5 seconds. Handle I2C open/ioctl/write/read errors and CRC failures gracefully by logging the error and continuing, and cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and log file on SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open, ioctl, read, write on /dev/i2c-1) to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor at address 0x25, for a ventilation system monitoring application. Use the continuous measurement command 0x362F, wait at least 1 ms, then read the 6-byte response (pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC), validating CRC-8 for both values (polynomial 0x31, init 0xFF). Convert raw pressure to Pa using the scale factor 240, and raw temperature to °C using the scale 200 with a -45 °C offset. Log pressure, temperature, and a timestamp, comma-separated, to 'airflow_data.txt'. Handle I2C write/read errors and sensor-absent paths gracefully, and clean up all resources (file descriptors, log files) on all exit paths, including SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Si7021 humidity and temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, and control a cooling fan on GPIO18 (active-high). Every 2 seconds, read temperature and humidity using the Hold Master measurement commands (0xE3 for temperature, 0xE5 for humidity), waiting at least 10 ms after each trigger before reading the 2-byte response. Convert raw values using temperature = 175.72 * raw / 65536.0 - 46.85 and humidity = 125.0 * raw / 65536.0 - 6.0. Log each reading with a timestamp into a 60-entry circular buffer and print it to stdout. Turn the fan ON when temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and OFF when it falls below 27.0 °C, with this hysteresis band. Retry failed I2C transactions up to 3 times, detect sensor-absent conditions, and degrade gracefully. Handle SIGINT cleanly: turn off the fan, close the I2C handle, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x62 (standard 100 kHz clock-stretching compatible settings), for monitoring indoor air quality in a smart ventilation system. Send the Start Periodic Measurement command (0x21B1) and wait at least 1 second before the first read attempt. Poll the data-ready flag (0xE4B8) before reading measurements, and only read data (0xEC05) once the flag indicates data is ready; read 9 bytes (6 data bytes plus 3 CRC bytes) and verify the CRC-8 checksum for each 2-byte word (polynomial 0x31, initialization 0xFF). CO2 in ppm is the raw value directly; convert temperature as -45 + 175 * raw/(2^16-1) and humidity as 100 * raw/(2^16-1). Note that the SCD40 requires ambient light for its photoacoustic measurement to function correctly. Every 5 seconds, log CO2, temperature, and humidity to 'air_quality.log' as CSV: timestamp,CO2_ppm,Temperature_C,Humidity_pct, flushing immediately. Check every return value from pigpio initialisation, I2C open, and command send; if any step or the CRC check fails, print a descriptive stderr message and retry or exit appropriately. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), send the Stop Periodic Measurement command (0x3F86), close the I2C handle, terminate pigpio, close the log file, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Sensirion SCD40 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x62, measuring CO2, temperature, and humidity. Use the command sequence start_periodic_measurement (0x21B1), poll get_data_ready_status (0xE4B8) until bit 0 is set, then read_measurement (0xEC05), which returns 9 bytes (3 words plus 3 CRC bytes); validate the CRC-8 checksum on each 2-byte data word. Send stop_periodic_measurement (0x3F86) on exit. Log each reading to a circular buffer in RAM with a capacity of 20 entries, and print each valid reading to stdout. Turn on an LED on GPIO17 when CO2 exceeds 1000 ppm, and turn it off otherwise. The measurement interval is 5 seconds. Verify pigpio and I2C initialisation, check every I2C write/read return value, validate every CRC-8 checksum, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths without crashing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for graceful shutdown that stops the sensor, closes the I2C handle, releases the GPIO, and terminates pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read temperature from an Analog Devices TMP05 digital temperature sensor connected to GPIO4 (physical pin 7). The TMP05 outputs a PWM-style signal where the ratio of high-time to total-cycle-time encodes the temperature; measure the high pulse width (TH) and total cycle width (TL) via busy-wait polling with microsecond-level timing, using gpioTick() for timestamps. Convert the reading to degrees Celsius using Temperature = 4215 - (2143 * TH / TL). Log each valid reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'temperature_log.txt' in append mode, sampling once every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialisation and file open results; detect sensor-absent or stuck-line conditions via a 50 ms timeout on each edge wait; guard against division by zero if TL is zero; flag readings outside the valid range -40 to +150 °C as errors; and after 3 consecutive failures, log a 'SENSOR MALFUNCTION' entry to the log file. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown, closing the file and releasing pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35-DIS-B sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x44, simulating a greenhouse environment monitor. Use the high-repeatability, clock-stretching-disabled measurement command (0x24, 0x00) and wait at least 15 ms before reading the 6-byte result. Validate the 8-bit CRC for both the temperature and humidity words; if the CRC fails or the I2C read/write fails, retry up to 3 times with a 1-second delay, and if all retries fail, log NaN values. Convert raw values to degrees Celsius and %RH using the standard Sensirion formulas, then add a simulated sinusoidal offset (±2 °C, ±5 %RH) over a 1-hour period to the actual readings. Log data in ISO-8601 UTC format to 'environmental_data.txt' every 5 seconds. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialisation, I2C open/read/write, and file open. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the standard Linux I2C i2c-dev interface to interface with a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa differential pressure sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Send the continuous measurement command (0x362F), wait for the conversion time of approximately 45 ms, and read 9 bytes containing pressure, temperature, and scale factor, each with an 8-bit CRC. Validate the CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial 0xFF) and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Convert the raw data to pressure in Pa and temperature in °C using the correct formulas. Log the timestamp, pressure, and temperature to a CSV file named 'airflow.csv' every 1 second. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM, ensuring the I2C file descriptor and any open file handles are properly closed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read temperature and humidity from a Sensirion SHT35-DIS-B sensor connected to I2C bus 1 at address 0x44 (ADDR pin tied to GND). Use the single-shot high-repeatability clock-stretching-disabled measurement command (0x2400); after sending it, wait at least 15 ms before reading 6 bytes (temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC, humidity MSB, humidity LSB, humidity CRC), validating both CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF). Convert raw values using T = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535 and RH = 100 * raw / 65535. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a CSV file named 'environment.csv' (columns: timestamp,temperature_c,humidity_pct), writing a header row if the file does not already exist or is empty, sampling every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialisation, I2C open, every I2C read/write, CRC validation, and file open; on failure print a descriptive error to stderr and continue or exit appropriately. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) to periodically read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit Si7021 sensor at I2C address 0x40 on bus 1 (GPIO 2/3), simulating a greenhouse monitoring system. Use the Si7021's No Hold Master measurement commands (0xF5 for humidity, 0xF3 for temperature), polling with read attempts until data is available or a 100 ms timeout is reached; read 3 bytes (MSB, LSB, CRC) for each measurement and verify the CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0x00). Use the paired-reading command 0xE0 to read the temperature associated with the previous humidity measurement. Convert raw values using Temperature = 175.72 * raw / 65536.0 - 46.85 and Humidity = 125.0 * raw / 65536.0 - 6.0. Every 5 seconds, log to a CSV file named 'environment.log' with the header 'timestamp,temperature_C,humidity_percent' using ISO-8601 timestamps; on an I2C or CRC error, log a line with 'ERROR' in place of the values and print a descriptive message to stderr, but continue running. Check every system call return value, handle sensor-absent (I2C open failure or NACK) and bus-error paths, and if a read fails, reset the sensor by writing the reset command (0xFE) before the next cycle. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to cleanly close the I2C file descriptor and exit gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, for a simplified HVAC airflow monitoring system. Use the continuous measurement command 0x362F, wait the specified conversion time, then read 9 bytes: pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC, and 3 scale factor bytes, validating CRC-8 for both the pressure and temperature raw values. Convert pressure using pressure = raw_pressure / scale_factor - 1000 (Pa), and temperature using temperature = raw_temperature / 200.0 - 45.0 (°C). Sample once per second and log each sample to 'airflow.dat' in binary format, with pressure and temperature each written as a float, keeping the file handle open across samples rather than reopening it on every write. Check pigpio initialisation, I2C open, command write, and read results, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Use signal handling (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for a graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the file on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, for a DIY ventilation system. Send the continuous measurement command 0x3603, wait the conversion time of 45 ms, then read 9 bytes (3 words plus 3 CRC bytes), validating each CRC-8 using polynomial 0x31. Convert the raw pressure using the scale factor 60.0 to Pa. Log each reading with a timestamp to 'pressure_log.txt' every 5 seconds. Handle I2C write/read errors, CRC failures, and sensor-absent scenarios gracefully without crashing the program. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate pigpio cleanly before the process exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure from a Honeywell Zephyr HAF Series HAFBLF0100A2AX5 digital airflow sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x28, and drives a PWM fan on GPIO18 (a hardware-PWM-capable pin) at 25 kHz based on the computed flow rate. The sensor operates on the heat transfer principle and returns a 16-bit word whose 2 most significant bits are status bits; mask them off and shift the result right by 2 to obtain the 14-bit raw flow reading. Convert the 14-bit reading to flow rate using the linear transfer function where 1638 counts correspond to 0 SLPM and 14745 counts correspond to 10 SLPM. Scale the fan's PWM duty cycle linearly between 0% at 0 SLPM and 100% at 10 SLPM. Sample the sensor every 100 ms and log each reading with a timestamp to flow_log.txt in the comma-separated format "timestamp,pressure_Pa\n". Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, logging errors to stderr without crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: turn off the fan, close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read pressure and temperature from an STMicroelectronics LPS33HW sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x5D. On startup, read the WHO_AM_I register (0x0F) and abort if it does not equal 0xB1. Configure CTRL_REG1 (0x10) to 0xB0 for block data update, 10 Hz output rate, and active mode. Read the 24-bit two's-complement pressure from PRESS_OUT_XL (0x28), PRESS_OUT_L (0x29), and PRESS_OUT_H (0x2A), storing it in an int32_t, and convert to hPa by dividing by 4096.0. Read the 16-bit two's-complement temperature from TEMP_OUT_L (0x2B) and TEMP_OUT_H (0x2C), storing it in an int16_t, and convert to Celsius using 42.5 + raw/480.0. Sample once per second using gpioDelay. Check the return value of every I2C read and write; on failure, write a timestamped error line to both stderr and the log file and continue the loop rather than exiting. Log each valid reading to environmental_data.txt, flushing after every write, in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Pressure: XXXX.XX hPa, Temperature: XX.XX °C" using localtime_r for thread-safe timestamp formatting. Handle SIGINT with a volatile sig_atomic_t flag that exits the main loop, then close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read an STLM75 digital temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x48, reading temperature register 0x00 once per second. The STLM75 returns a 16-bit two's-complement word with 9-bit resolution (sign bit, 8 data bits, and the low 7 bits always 0); because pigpio's i2cReadWordData returns bytes in little-endian order, swap the two bytes before extracting the value, then right-shift by 7 and divide by 2 to get degrees Celsius. Store each reading in a 10-element circular buffer in memory and compute the running average. Turn on an LED on GPIO 17 when the average temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turn it off otherwise. Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, and every I2C read; if a read fails, skip that iteration and continue. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so the program shuts down cleanly, turning off the LED, closing the I2C handle, and calling gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cClose, i2cReadDevice, i2cWriteDevice, gpioTerminate) to interface with a Sensirion SCD30 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x61. Set the measurement interval to 2 seconds and start continuous measurement with ambient pressure compensation disabled (0). Before each read, poll the data-ready flag with command 0x0202, then read the measurement with command 0x0300, returning 18 bytes (3 values of 4 data bytes plus 2 CRC bytes each). Implement the SCD30 CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) for every write command that carries arguments and verify the CRC on every value read. Log CO2 (ppm), temperature (°C), and humidity (%RH) with ISO 8601 UTC timestamps as comma-separated values to air_quality.log, flushing after each write, and drive a simulated ventilation system from the CO2 reading: OFF below 800 ppm, LOW between 800 and 1199 ppm, and HIGH at 1200 ppm or above. Handle every error path — pigpio initialization failure, I2C open/write/read failures, sensor non-response, data-not-ready, and CRC mismatches — by logging the error and continuing the loop rather than crashing. Use sigaction to catch SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop periodic measurement, close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate(). In a mocked or emulated environment where the I2C hardware may be absent, initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus, and if sensor initialization or reads fail, log the error and exit gracefully with code 0 rather than crashing or returning a nonzero status.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to periodically read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP32 (±125 Pa) sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x21. Send the continuous-measurement command bytes 0x36, 0x2F to start the sensor, then poll 9 bytes per reading: pressure MSB, pressure LSB, pressure CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC, scale-factor MSB, scale-factor LSB, and scale-factor CRC. Verify the CRC-8 checksum on the pressure, temperature, and scale-factor words, and convert the raw pressure using pressure_pa = raw_pressure / scale_factor. Log each timestamped reading to the console at a default sampling interval of 1000 ms, configurable via a command-line argument. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, including sensor-absent and bus-error paths; if the sensor is not physically connected, detect the I2C read/write failures and exit with a clear diagnostic message rather than crashing. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths through signal handling, and make sure the program compiles and runs cleanly in a mocked or emulated environment, exiting with code 0 when terminated by SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read differential pressure and temperature from a Sensirion SDP810-125Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 (SDA on GPIO 2, SCL on GPIO 3) at address 0x25. Send the continuous-measurement command 0x3615, wait at least 45 ms for the conversion, then read 9 bytes containing the pressure, temperature, and their scale factors. Validate the CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) on each 3-byte data word, then convert the raw values using the per-reading scale factors returned by the sensor: raw_pressure / scale_factor_pressure for pressure, and raw_temperature / 200.0 for temperature. Log the results to stdout every 1 second. Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, and every read and write, and handle CRC mismatches and sensor-absent or bus-error paths without crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64-bit kernel to periodically read temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC1000 sensor on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2 = SDA, GPIO 3 = SCL) at its default 7-bit address 0x40, using the Linux i2c-dev API (open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) rather than the deprecated wiringPi library. Configure the Configuration Register (pointer 0x02), setting bit 12 to enable a combined temperature-and-humidity measurement at 14-bit resolution. To read a sample, write the temperature register pointer 0x00 to the sensor, wait at least 20 ms for the 14-bit conversion (the DRDYn pin is not connected, so rely on this fixed delay), then read 4 bytes — 2 bytes temperature followed by 2 bytes humidity — in a single I2C read transaction. Convert the raw 16-bit values using Temperature (°C) = (raw / 65536.0) * 165.0 - 40.0 and Humidity (%RH) = (raw / 65536.0) * 100.0. Check the return value of every open(), ioctl(), read(), and write() call, and handle the sensor-absent path where the device file cannot be opened or the sensor fails to acknowledge. Log readings to the console every 5 seconds in the format "Temperature: XX.XX C, Humidity: XX.XX %"; on a read failure, print an error to stderr and continue the loop without exiting. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM so the program closes the I2C file descriptor and exits cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read pressure and temperature from a TDK ICP-10101 barometric pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x63. On startup, read the 4 calibration coefficients from the sensor's OTP memory with command 0x50 (8 bytes) and compute the scale_factor_lut, scale_factor_h, and scale_factor_p scaling factors per the datasheet. Every 5 seconds, trigger a high-precision measurement with command 0x40, wait 7 ms, then read 6 bytes — 2 bytes temperature followed by 4 bytes pressure — and apply the datasheet compensation formulas to convert the raw values to Celsius and Pascals. Log each reading to stdout with an ISO-8601 timestamp, for example "2024-01-15T14:30:00 - Temperature: 22.45 C, Pressure: 101325.00 Pa". Check the return value of every pigpio I2C call, detect a sensor-absent condition when a read returns a negative value or all bytes are 0xFF, and log such errors to stderr without crashing. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Linux i2c-dev interface (open() and ioctl() on /dev/i2c-1) to periodically read pressure values from a Melexis MLX90819 (digital I2C version) sensor on I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x60. Trigger a measurement and read the 16-bit raw pressure value from the sensor's pressure registers, MSB at 0xAA and LSB at 0xAB, once per second. Convert the raw value to kPa using a linear scaling factor of 0.1. Log each reading to stdout with a timestamp. Handle I2C communication failures, including read/write errors and a sensor-absent condition, by printing to stderr and continuing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so the program exits cleanly on Ctrl+C, closing the I2C file descriptor.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open() and ioctl()) rather than the deprecated wiringPi library to interface with a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa differential pressure sensor connected on I2C bus 1, with SDA on GPIO 2 and SCL on GPIO 3, at address 0x25, for a do-it-yourself HVAC airflow monitoring system. Send the continuous-measurement command 0x362F, wait 45 ms, then read 9 bytes forming 3 words: pressure, temperature, and their CRCs. Validate each word's CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert the raw values using pressure = raw / 60.0 (Pa) and temperature = raw / 200.0 (C). Log the timestamp, differential pressure, and temperature as comma-separated values to pressure_log.txt. Handle I2C open/write/read errors and sensor-absent paths gracefully, and release all resources cleanly on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read differential pressure data from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Use the continuous-measurement command bytes 0x36, 0x2F to trigger readings, wait at least 8 ms for the measurement to complete, then read 3 bytes: 2 data bytes plus 1 CRC byte. Verify the CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) of the data bytes, and convert the raw 16-bit signed value to pressure in Pa using raw / 60.0. Check every pigpio I2C call, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Log the pressure reading and a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) once per second as comma-separated values to a CSV file named airflow_log.csv, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (i2cOpen, i2cReadI2CBlockData, i2cClose) to interface with a Melexis MLX90821 relative pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, simulating a tire pressure monitoring system. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus with error checking. Verify the sensor identity by reading the WHO_AM_I register at 0x08 and checking for the value 0x08, then read the 4 calibration coefficients from registers 0x05-0x08 using i2cReadI2CBlockData. In a loop, trigger a measurement by writing 0x00 to register 0x00, wait 10 ms, then read 6 bytes of pressure and temperature data from register 0x00, converting them to hPa and Celsius using the ICP-10110 datasheet formulas. Sample every 5 seconds, logging each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to environmental_data.txt in append mode (flushing after each write) and printing it to stdout. Handle I2C read/write errors by printing to stderr and skipping the sample. Handle SIGINT gracefully: set a flag to exit the loop, close the I2C handle, close the file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads a TDK ICP-10125 barometric pressure sensor over I2C using the standard Linux I2C interface (open(), ioctl(), read(), write() on <linux/i2c-dev.h>) at the sensor's default address 0x63, and drives a warning LED using the libgpiod API, without using wiringPi. Read the 4 calibration coefficients from OTP memory register 0x66, then trigger a measurement by writing command 0x4011 (high-accuracy mode). After a 20 ms delay, read 6 bytes — 2 bytes pressure, 2 bytes temperature, and 2 bytes CRC — verifying the CRC, and apply the official InvenSense ICP-10125 conversion formulas to compute pressure in Pascals and temperature in Celsius. Poll the sensor once per second. Using libgpiod, request an LED line on GPIO 17 (BCM numbering) as output and blink it at 1 Hz (500 ms on, 500 ms off) under normal conditions; when the pressure drops below 95000 Pa, indicating high altitude, blink it at 5 Hz (100 ms on, 100 ms off) as a warning. Check every I2C syscall, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and verify the CRC on every read. Handle SIGINT to release the GPIO line and close the I2C file descriptor cleanly on all exit paths.

Read ambient temperature from RAM register 0x06 and object temperature from RAM register 0x07, converting each raw 16-bit value to Celsius using temp = raw * 0.02 - 273.15. Every 2 seconds, log the timestamped readings to temperature_log.txt, skipping the log entry if a reading is invalid. Control a cooling fan on GPIO 18 with hysteresis: turn it on when the object temperature exceeds 30 °C and off when it falls below 28 °C. Validate pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, and every I2C read/write; retry a failed read up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between attempts. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly by closing the I2C handle, turning off the fan, and terminating pigpio.

Accept incoming HTTP connections and respond with a simple HTML page showing the current temperature and humidity. I have written a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID-controlled reflow oven using a MAX6675 thermocouple over SPI0 (CE0/CE1) and a solid-state relay on GPIO17, reading a target temperature profile from profile.txt (lines of time_seconds,target_temp_celsius). Use libgpiod for GPIO control and spidev for SPI communication. The MAX6675 returns a 16-bit word where bit 2 is the open-circuit flag and bits 3-14 hold the 12-bit temperature; read it at 1 Hz. The PID controller's output, from 0.0 to 1.0, sets the solid-state relay's duty cycle over each 1-second period. Log temperature data to reflow_log.csv. Implement robust error handling for SPI communication and GPIO control, including sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths through signal handling.

Create a new log file each day at midnight with CSV header 'Timestamp,Temperature(C),Humidity(%),MotionDetected'. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. Build with: gcc -o logger logger.c -lgpiod -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod library, through the Linux GPIO character-device interface, to monitor a YL-83 rain sensor connected on GPIO17, reading it as an active-low digital output where a value of 0 means rain has been detected, polling the line every 2 seconds. When rain is detected, close a window by driving an L298N motor driver board, with its enable line ENA on GPIO22, its first direction input IN1 on GPIO23, and its second direction input IN2 on GPIO24, so that the motor runs forward for 5 seconds and then stops. Check the return value of every libgpiod call, and explicitly handle the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened at startup. Ensure the motor is stopped and every requested GPIO line is released back to the system on program exit, whether that exit is triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM signal handling, and log each event with a timestamp to stdout. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to control a PWM-driven cooling fan on GPIO18 (BCM), adjusting fan speed based on CPU temperature read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp. Use a linear mapping: 0% duty at 40°C, 100% duty at 70°C, clamped below 40°C and above 70°C. Set the PWM frequency to 25 kHz with a 0-255 duty range. Log timestamp, temperature, and duty cycle to fan_log.txt every 5 seconds. Handle file write errors, temperature read failures, and pigpio initialization failures gracefully. Clean up all resources on SIGINT/SIGTERM — stop the fan, close files, and terminate pigpio. Do not use wiringPi or ZeroMQ.
raw:
```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define FAN_PIN 18
#define FAN_FREQ 25000
#define FAN_MIN 0
#define FAN_MAX 255
#define FAN_TEMP_MIN 40
#define FAN_TEMP_MAX 70
#define FAN_LOG_FILE "fan_log.txt"
#define FAN_LOG_INTERVAL 5

static volatile int running = 1;

void sig_handler(int signo)
{
    if (signo == SIGINT || signo == SIGTERM) {
        running = 0;
    }
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    int fan_duty = 0;
    int fan_temp = 0;
    FILE *fan_log = NULL;
    char fan_log_line[100];
    char *fan_log_timestamp = NULL;
    char *fan_log_temp = NULL;
    char *fan_log_duty = NULL;

    signal(SIGINT, sig_handler);
    signal(SIGTERM, sig_handler);

    if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "pigpio initialization failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    gpioSetMode(FAN_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);
    gpioSetPWMfrequency(FAN_PIN, FAN_FREQ);
    gpioSetPWMrange(FAN_PIN, FAN_MAX);

    fan_log = fopen(FAN_LOG_FILE, "w");
    if (fan_log == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "failed to open fan log file\n");
        return 1;
    }

    while (running) {
        fan_temp = (int) (1000 * (float) (gpioRead(4) / 1000));
        fan_duty = (int) (255 * (float) (fan_temp - FAN_TEMP_MIN) / (FAN_TEMP_MAX - FAN_TEMP_MIN));
        if (fan_duty < FAN_MIN) {
            fan_duty = FAN_MIN;
        } else if (fan_duty > FAN_MAX) {
            fan_duty = FAN_MAX;
        }
        gpioPWM(FAN_PIN, fan_duty);

        fan_log_timestamp = ctime(&time(NULL));
        fan_log_temp = malloc(10);
        sprintf(fan_log_temp, "%d", fan_temp);
        fan_log_duty = malloc(10);
        sprintf(fan_log_duty, "%d", fan_duty);
        sprintf(fan_log_line, "%s %s %s\n", fan_log_timestamp, fan_log_temp, fan_log_duty);
        fputs(fan_log_line, fan_log);
        free(fan_log_temp);
        free(fan_log_duty);

        sleep(FAN_LOG_INTERVAL);
    }

    gpioTerminate();
    fclose(fan_log);

    return 0;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor over I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA=GPIO2/pin3, SCL=GPIO3/pin5) and logs readings with timestamps to weather_data.txt in append mode, using only the Linux i2c-dev interface (no wiringPi, no pigpio). The default BMP280 address is 0x76 (SDO tied to GND); also try 0x77 as a fallback. The sensor is powered from the 3V3 rail, never 5V. Read chip_id from register 0xD0 and verify it equals 0x58, aborting with a clear error if it does not match, then read the 24-byte calibration block starting at register 0x88 (dig_T1..dig_P9) and apply the Bosch 64-bit compensation formulas. Configure ctrl_meas (register 0xF4) for forced mode with oversampling x1 for temperature and pressure, re-writing ctrl_meas each loop to trigger each measurement, and poll the status register (0xF3) bit 3 (measuring) until it clears, with a timeout, before reading 6 bytes of raw data from register 0xF7 (press_msb) and combining into 20-bit values. Log every 5 seconds in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa'. Check every I/O call — open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs — and handle failures gracefully. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to exit the loop cleanly, closing the I2C file descriptor and exiting 0. If the sensor disappears mid-run, log the error to stderr and attempt to continue or exit gracefully.

Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature from an LM75 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x48 using the libgpiod library (never wiringPi). Read the 16-bit temperature register (0x00) every 1 second; the value arrives two's-complement, MSB first, left-shifted by 5 bits (bits [15:5] hold the temperature, bits [4:0] are always 0), so divide the signed 16-bit value by 256.0 to get degrees Celsius. Log each reading to an in-memory circular buffer with a capacity of 60 samples and compute the running average. Trigger an LED on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering) if the temperature exceeds 28.0°C, turning it off otherwise. Use a background thread with a mutex-protected circular buffer for data acquisition. Check every I2C read/write and GPIO init call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging to stderr and attempting re-initialization, and ensure clean resource release — close the I2C file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, destroy the mutex — on all exit paths including SIGINT.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that regulates a resistive heater connected through a logic-level MOSFET on GPIO18 (hardware PWM) using the pigpio library (not wiringPi). Measure temperature with a PT100 RTD through a MAX31865 RTD-to-digital converter over SPI0 (CE0, SPI mode 1, 500 kHz), using a 430-ohm reference resistor for the PT100 (nominal resistance 100 ohms). Initialize the MAX31865 by writing 0xC1 to the configuration register (0x80) to enable VBIAS, enable auto-conversion, and clear faults. Read the 15-bit RTD code from registers 0x01 (MSB) and 0x02 (LSB), check the fault bit (D0 of MSB), and read the fault status register (0x07) to diagnose open, over-voltage, or under-voltage faults. Convert the RTD code to resistance using R_rtd = (code / 32768) * R_ref, then convert resistance to temperature using the Callendar-Van Dusen equation R = R0 * (1 + A*t + B*t^2), solved for t, for t >= 0. Run a PID control loop every 100 ms, outputting a PWM duty cycle on GPIO18 at 1 kHz with pigpio range 1000 for 0-100% duty. Include a failsafe shutoff: if temperature exceeds 80°C, an SPI read fails, or any MAX31865 fault is detected, immediately set PWM duty to 0 and exit with an error. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully — turn off the heater, close SPI, terminate pigpio, exit cleanly. Load the target temperature and PID gains (Kp, Ki, Kd) from a JSON config file at startup, using defaults target=25°C, Kp=1.0, Ki=0.1, Kd=0.01 if the file is missing. Log errors to stderr and exit with nonzero status on critical failures.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod API (not sysfs or wiringPi) to sample the analog audio output of an Adafruit MAX9814 Electret Microphone Amplifier. Connect the MAX9814 OUT pin to GPIO 17 (configured as input) and the GAIN pin to GPIO 18 (configured as output), setting GPIO 18 LOW to select 60dB gain. Since the MAX9814 provides an analog signal, rapidly poll the digital input pin, at a 10 ms interval, to detect rising edges (logic HIGH) as peak sound events. Log each detected peak to audio_log.txt with a timestamp formatted as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL', where LEVEL is 1 for a rising edge. Handle all libgpiod initialization and I/O errors robustly, checking the return value of every API call, and ensure clean release of all libgpiod resources on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. Print a startup message and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to monitor flow rate from a Sensirion SLF3S-4000B Liquid Flow Sensor connected on I2C bus 1 at the default 7-bit address 0x36, for a microfluidic drug delivery system. Initialize the sensor by sending the 2-byte command 0x3608 to start continuous measurement. Every 1000 ms, read 3 bytes from the sensor: a 16-bit raw flow value (MSB first) followed by a CRC-8 byte, and validate it using the Sensirion CRC-8 algorithm (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF); if the CRC check fails, log an error and skip that reading. Convert the raw 16-bit signed value to a flow rate in uL/min by dividing by 1000.0. Log each valid reading to a CSV file named 'flow_log.csv' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,flow_rate_uL_min', opening the file once at startup in append mode, keeping it open, and flushing after each write rather than reopening repeatedly. Check every pigpio initialization, I2C open, write, and read call; on an I2C read or write failure, log the error to stderr and attempt to recover on the next loop iteration. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with a Honeywell MICS-VZ-89TE VOC sensor connected on I2C bus 1 at address 0x70. Read the 7-byte sensor state starting at register 0x00, extracting TVOC (ppb) from bytes 1-2 and eCO2 (ppm) from bytes 5-6 (big-endian), and compute an IAQ index using the formula IAQ = clamp(100 - (TVOC / 10.0) - ((eCO2 - 400) / 50.0), 0, 100). Every 5 seconds, log a timestamped line with the IAQ, TVOC, and eCO2 values to 'air_quality_log.csv'. Check every I2C read and write return value, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions without crashing. Handle SIGINT gracefully by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod v1 API to monitor a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, active-high): the sensor outputs HIGH while touched and LOW when released. Open gpiochip0 by name and request the line as input with the consumer label "ttp223_tamper". Poll the line every 100 ms using CLOCK_MONOTONIC. If the sensor remains continuously touched for more than 5 seconds, print an intrusion alert to stdout once per touch event (not repeatedly), and reset the timer when the sensor is released. Check every libgpiod call for failure and print strerror(errno) on error; if a sensor read fails mid-loop, print an error and exit with EXIT_FAILURE after cleanup. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing the line and closing the chip on all exit paths. Do not use sysfs or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to continuously sample audio data from the InvenSense INMP441 I2S MEMS microphone and log 16-bit PCM samples to a raw file named 'audio_capture.pcm'. The INMP441 outputs 24-bit data left-justified in a 32-bit frame; extract the 24-bit data and right-shift it to produce 16-bit PCM samples. Acquire the I2S data through the Linux ALSA subsystem (via /dev/snd/pcmC0D0c or the snd-pcm kernel interface). Use the libgpiod library to drive the microphone's L/R select pin on GPIO 17 to select the left channel. Handle I2S initialization, data acquisition, and file I/O errors robustly, and implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a SainSmart IR Flame Sensor Module (LM393 comparator, IR photodiode) connected to GPIO 4 (digital DO pin), which outputs LOW when a flame is detected and HIGH when no flame is present. Poll the sensor every 50 ms with 50 ms software debouncing. When a flame is detected, drive a PWM-controlled cooling fan on GPIO 18 using hardware PWM at 100 Hz, scaling the duty cycle from 0 to 80% based on flame duration using an exponential curve; turn the fan off immediately when no flame is detected. Continuously read the 16-bit result register (0x00), unpack the exponent (bits 15-12) and mantissa (bits 11-0), and compute lux as 0.01 * 2^exponent * mantissa. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM, ensuring the I2C bus handle, pigpio library, and any open file handles are properly released on all exit paths.

Poll all 8 channels every 50 ms and log the binary state of each channel to the console in CSV format with an ISO-8601 timestamp, one line per poll cycle, running until interrupted. Install a SIGINT handler for graceful shutdown on Ctrl+C.

Install a SIGINT (Ctrl+C) handler so the program exits cleanly and always calls gpioTerminate() on every exit path. During initialization, verify the sensor's PART ID (0x45), write 0x17 to the HW_KEY register, configure the CHLIST register (0x01) to enable UV and ALS_VIS, and use the ALS_FORCE command (0x06) to trigger measurements. Every 1 second, continuously read UV index and Visible ALS data, print the readings to the console, and log them to a CSV file named 'uv_als_log.csv' with columns timestamp, uv_index, als_visible. Handle potential I2C errors and sensor-absent/bus-error paths gracefully. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to read flow rates from two Sensirion SLF3S-0600F Liquid Flow Sensors on I2C at addresses 0x36 and 0x37, using the Linux I2C character-device API (open()/ioctl() on /dev/i2c-1) for I2C communication and the libgpiod library for GPIO control. Initialize each sensor by sending the start-measurement command 0x3608 to I2C command register 0x08 and wait 100 ms for the first measurement. Read 9 bytes from register 0x00 (three 3-byte measurements: flow, temperature, CRC), validating each flow measurement with the Sensirion 8-bit CRC (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF); on an I2C error or CRC failure, log the error and skip that sensor's reading for the cycle. Convert the raw 16-bit signed flow value to ml/min using a scale factor of 0.036. Every 1 second, log the average flow rate of the two sensors to 'flow_log.txt', and drive an alarm on GPIO 17 high when that average is below 0.5 ml/min and low otherwise. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: release the GPIO lines, close the I2C file descriptors, and close the log file. Loop continuously with a 1-second interval between reads.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to poll a KY-033 Obstacle Avoidance Sensor Module connected to GPIO 4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7), which outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected within its threshold and HIGH (1) otherwise. Initialize pigpio and verify success, printing an error to stderr and returning non-zero on failure. Configure GPIO 4 as input with the internal pull-up resistor enabled and poll it every 50 ms. On each detection (reading == 0), record a timestamp and the reading into a circular buffer of 100 entries that overwrites the oldest entry when full, and print an alert to stdout. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), print the entire buffer contents in chronological order with human-readable timestamps, release all pigpio resources, and exit cleanly. Do not use any deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 (64-bit Bookworm) that interfaces with an Omron D7S vibration sensor over I2C (up to 400 kHz, default 7-bit address 0x55) using the Linux I2C character-device API (open()/ioctl(I2C_SLAVE)/read()/write() on /dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) to detect subtle vibrations indicating pre-failure in a small cooling fan. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x10 to register 0x1D (MODE_CONTROL) to switch it from standby to active mode, then wait until the operating-status register (0x1B) bit 0 reads 1; if the sensor does not become active within 1 second, print an error and exit. Every 500 ms, read the 16-bit signed acceleration registers X (0x2A/0x2B), Y (0x2C/0x2D), and Z (0x2E/0x2F), little-endian with LSB first, and convert the raw values to g using the scaling factor 0.0009765625 g/LSB. Log each sample as a CSV row with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'fan_health.csv' in append mode, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Check every I2C syscall return value; on a read/write/ioctl failure, print a diagnostic to stderr and retry on the next iteration rather than crashing. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file, then exit. The program should run until interrupted by the user.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with two Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance sensors (active-LOW outputs, logic 0 = obstacle detected) connected to GPIO 23 (Sensor 1 OUT) and GPIO 24 (Sensor 2 OUT), triggering an LED on GPIO 25 (through a 220-330 ohm resistor to GND) when an obstacle is detected within approximately 10 cm of either sensor. Poll both sensors every 100 ms. Turn the LED ON immediately when either sensor reads LOW, and turn it OFF when both read HIGH. Verify pigpio initialization, validate every gpioSetMode/gpioRead/gpioWrite return code, and ensure clean resource release (gpioTerminate) on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define SENSOR1_PIN 23
#define SENSOR2_PIN 24
#define LED_PIN 25

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    int sensor1_value, sensor2_value, led_value;
    int sensor1_state, sensor2_state, led_state;

    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "pigpio initialisation failed\n");
        return 1;
    }

    gpioSetMode(SENSOR1_PIN, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetMode(SENSOR2_PIN, PI_INPUT);
    gpioSetMode(LED_PIN, PI_OUTPUT);

    sensor1_state = 0;
    sensor2_state = 0;
    led_state = 0;

    while (1)
    {
        sensor1_value = gpioRead(SENSOR1_PIN);
        sensor2_value = gpioRead(SENSOR2_PIN);

        if (sensor1_value == 0 && sensor2_value == 0)
        {
            if (led_state == 0)
            {
                gpioWrite(LED_PIN, 1);
                led_state = 1;
            }
        }
        else
        {
            if (led_state == 1)
            {
                gpioWrite(LED_PIN, 0);
                led_state = 0;
            }
        }

        usleep(100000);
    }

    gpioTerminate();

    return 0;
}

The sensor output is connected to physical pin 7 (Broadcom GPIO 4), configured as input with the internal pull-up resistor enabled. Count rising-edge pulses in a 1-second window using an atomic add for the pulse counter, and compute RPM as pulses_per_second * 60, assuming one pulse per revolution. Every 1-second sample, log 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS <rpm>' to 'rpm_log.txt' (flushing the file after each write) and print it to stdout, logging RPM 0 rather than aborting when the sensor is absent or not rotating. Check every pigpio call and file-open call for errors and exit with a diagnostic message on failure. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers so Ctrl+C stops cleanly: disable the timer and alert callback, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to detect direction of rotation from two Melexis MLX90217 unipolar Hall-effect sensors connected to GPIO 17 (Sensor A) and GPIO 27 (Sensor B) via hardware pull-up resistors, physically offset by 90 degrees to produce a quadrature signal. Use pigpio alerts (gpioSetAlertFunc) for edge-triggered interrupts instead of polling, and implement a quadrature state machine that tracks the previous state to determine direction, protecting the shared state between the ISR and main loop with a mutex. Log each detected rotation event (CW or CCW) with a millisecond-precision timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm) to 'rotation_log.txt'. Check all error paths: gpioInitialise(), gpioSetAlertFunc(), gpioSetPullUpDown(), and file open. Use a signal handler (SIGINT/SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown, ensuring the log file is flushed/closed and pigpio is terminated. The main loop should wait on a condition variable or sleep, not busy-spin. Never use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library's line request API to interface with a SainSmart TTP223B digital capacitive touch sensor whose OUT pin is connected to GPIO 23 (physical pin 16), and an LED on GPIO 18 (physical pin 12) with a current-limiting resistor. Poll the touch sensor every 50 ms (to avoid busy-waiting) and illuminate the LED only while the sensor is actively touched. Check all libgpiod calls, including chip opening, line requests, reads, and writes, handling the case where the GPIO chip is unavailable. Log all touch events, errors, and startup/shutdown messages to the system syslog using openlog/syslog. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers to ensure the LED is turned off and resources are released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library's line event interface to read touch input from a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11), which outputs HIGH (3.3 V) when touched and LOW when idle. On each rising-edge touch detection (with approximately 50 ms software debounce), toggle an LED connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12). Initialize the LED line as output and drive it LOW at startup. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully: release all libgpiod resources (lines and chip) and exit cleanly.

Log timestamps and sensor state changes to a CSV file named 'shaft_log.txt' in the format 'timestamp,sensor1_state,sensor2_state'. Handle potential GPIO initialization and file I/O errors gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C). Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read heart rate and SpO2 data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 I2C-based optical sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x28. Initialize pigpio, open the I2C bus, and verify the sensor is present by reading the PART_ID register at 0x00. Configure the sensor for continuous measurement by writing to the CONFIG register at 0x30. Once per second, read heart rate data from register 0x02 and SpO2 data from register 0x04, and log each reading with a timestamp in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Heart Rate: X BPM, SpO2: Y%%' to 'biometric_log.txt' in append mode, flushing after each write. Check every I2C read/write return value and handle failures; on communication errors, print a message to stderr and continue the loop. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and log file and terminating pigpio before exiting.

Connect an active-high alarm (buzzer/LED) to GPIO 27, initialized LOW. Poll at a 100 ms interval using gpioDelay. Log all tilt-start, threshold-exceeded, and tilt-end events with ISO-8601 timestamps (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS) to 'bridge_integrity.log'. Check pigpio initialization, log file opening, and gpioRead return values. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown (deactivate the alarm, close the log file, call gpioTerminate), ensuring the alarm is deactivated on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod character-device API (gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_chip_get_line, gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_request_output, gpiod_line_get_value, gpiod_line_set_value on device 'gpiochip0'; not wiringPi or sysfs) to implement a flame-detection safety system with a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor and an active buzzer. The KY-026 digital-output pin is connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11) and is active-low: it reads LOW when a flame is detected and HIGH otherwise. An active buzzer is connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) and sounds when its control line is driven HIGH. Poll the flame sensor every 500 ms. On a HIGH-to-LOW transition (software edge detection, not continuously while the line stays LOW), log the event with a timestamp to 'alert_log.txt' and activate the buzzer for 2 seconds, then continue. Log a 'System started' entry at startup and a 'System stopped' entry on clean shutdown. Break the 2-second buzzer activation and the 500 ms poll interval into 100 ms slices so the program can respond promptly to shutdown signals. Check every libgpiod call, file operation, and syscall for failure, printing a diagnostic via strerror(errno) to stderr and exiting non-zero if initialization fails. Include the headers errno.h, string.h, time.h, signal.h, unistd.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h, and gpiod.h. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: turn the buzzer off, release the lines, close the chip, close the log file, and exit cleanly with code 0. Build with: gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 -o flame_alert flame_alert.c -lgpiod.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to interface with three Texas Instruments TMAG5110A1 Hall-effect latch magnetic sensors on GPIO4, GPIO17, and GPIO27 (BCM numbering). Each sensor's open-drain OUT pin drives a GPIO input with an internal pull-up enabled: it pulls low when a south pole is present and releases high otherwise, so a logic low means magnet-present and a logic high means magnet-removed. Initialize pigpio and verify every GPIO mode and pull call returns 0. Poll all three sensors every 100 ms using gpioDelay, and on the first read record the initial state without falsely logging a transition. Log each state change, with an ISO-8601 timestamp and sensor identifier, to 'magnet_log.txt'. Handle sensor read errors gracefully by logging to stderr and continuing. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for clean shutdown that close the log file and call gpioTerminate(). Include comments explaining the latch behavior.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read heart-rate data from a Silicon Labs Si1182-A-GM optical heart-rate sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x4A. Initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus, checking every return code. Verify the sensor's PART_ID register (0x00) reads 0x02 and HW_REV register (0x01) reads 0x01, aborting with a clear error if the sensor is absent or wrong. Configure the sensor by writing the LED current (0x3F), averaging (0x04), and enable (0x01) registers, checking each write. Read the 16-bit heart-rate register (0x2A) once per second using i2cReadWordData and convert the raw value to BPM using raw * 0.5. Apply a 5-sample moving average and validate that the filtered BPM is between 30 and 220 before logging. Append valid readings as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,BPM' to heart_rate.csv with an immediate flush. Retry on transient I2C read errors without crashing, and implement robust error handling for sensor-absent and bus-error conditions throughout. Handle SIGINT gracefully, closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library (never wiringPi) to monitor a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor whose digital-output pin is connected to GPIO17 (Broadcom pin 17, physical pin 11). The sensor's DO pin is active-low: it reads LOW when flame is detected and HIGH when clear. Configure the line as input with an internal pull-up and poll it every 100 ms. When a falling edge is detected (HIGH-to-LOW transition, edge-triggered rather than level-triggered, to avoid duplicate alerts while the signal remains LOW), print 'FLAME DETECTED' to the console and append a line with the current timestamp and 'FLAME DETECTED' to 'flame_log.txt' in append mode, flushing immediately. Check every libgpiod call and file operation, and handle the case where the GPIO chip or line is unavailable. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for graceful shutdown that releases the GPIO line, closes the chip, and closes the log file on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the libgpiod v2+ bulk/config API (not sysfs, not wiringPi, not the deprecated libgpiod v1 simple API: gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_line_config_new, gpiod_line_settings_new, gpiod_line_settings_set_direction, gpiod_line_config_add_line_settings, gpiod_chip_request_lines, gpiod_line_request_get_value, gpiod_line_request_set_value, gpiod_line_request_release) to read an 8-channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module and display an 8-bit binary counter on GPIO outputs. Connect TTP226 outputs OUT1-OUT8, each active-high (3.3 V touched, 0 V idle), to GPIO 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 respectively (BCM numbering), and drive the counter display on GPIO17 (bit 0, LSB) through GPIO24 (bit 7, MSB). Poll the sensor lines every 10 ms, tracking each line's previous state to detect rising edges (inactive-to-active) without double-counting while held; on each new touch, increment an 8-bit counter that wraps 255 to 0 and immediately update the 8 output GPIOs so bit b appears on GPIO 17+b. Log every touch event to 'touch_log.txt' in append mode as 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ, Channel: <1-8>, Counter: <0-255>' and also print 'Touch on channel <N> | Counter: <V>' to stdout. Include a 200 ms stabilization delay after requesting lines before entering the main loop. Check every libgpiod call, file open, and I/O operation, reporting errors with strerror(errno); if gpiod_chip_open fails, print an error and exit non-zero; if any line-request call fails, release everything acquired so far and exit non-zero; if a sensor read errors, log to stderr and skip that channel without crashing; if an output write fails, log to stderr and continue; if the log file cannot be opened, log a warning to stderr and continue with stdout output. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by resetting all output pins to 0, releasing all libgpiod resources, closing the chip, and exiting cleanly with status 0. Build with: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o touch_counter touch_counter.c -lgpiod.

1. Connect the TTP226 sensor to the Raspberry Pi

Open gpiochip0 and request all 8 lines as inputs. Poll every 200 ms and log each channel's state (0 or 1) to the console in a single timestamped line using a monotonic clock, for example '[12.345s] CH1=0 CH2=1 CH3=0 CH4=0 CH5=0 CH6=0 CH7=0 CH8=0'. Handle errors at every step, including chip-open failure, line-request failure, and individual line-read failure, printing to stderr and exiting with non-zero status. Because the LED is common-anode, invert every PWM duty-cycle value as 255 minus the value, and clamp all color channel values to [0, 255]. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient light from a BH1750 I2C sensor at address 0x23 and adjusts the brightness of an APA102 LED strip via SPI proportionally to the measured lux. Use the Linux I2C (/dev/i2c-1) and SPI (/dev/spidev0.0) character devices directly; do not use the deprecated wiringPi library. Initialize the BH1750 in One-Time High-Resolution mode (command 0x20), wait approximately 120 ms for the conversion to complete, then read the 2-byte result and convert to lux using lux = raw / 1.2. Map the lux range [10, 300] to the APA102's 5-bit global brightness [0, 31]. Send an APA102 frame consisting of a 32-bit zero start frame, one 32-bit LED frame per LED (0xE0 | brightness, blue, green, red), and a 32-bit 0xFF end frame, using a 1 MHz SPI clock. Handle SIGINT gracefully by turning off the LEDs and closing all file descriptors. Implement robust error handling for all I/O operations, sensor-absent scenarios, and bus errors.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for both I2C communication and SPI output to control an APA102 RGB LED strip's overall brightness based on ambient light from up to three BH1750 I2C light sensors on I2C bus 1, at addresses 0x23 (ADDR low) and 0x5C (ADDR high); attempt to open both addresses and gracefully skip any sensor that is not present. The APA102 strip connects via hardware SPI: MOSI on GPIO10 and SCLK on GPIO11. Initialize each BH1750 using the One-Time High-Resolution Mode 2 command (0x21), wait approximately 180 ms for the conversion to complete, and read 2 bytes of data. Average the lux readings across available sensors, ignoring any that report read errors, and map the average lux to a global brightness level (0-31) for the strip, where lower ambient light yields higher brightness. Smoothly fade the strip's global brightness to the new target over 500 ms, looping continuously with a 100 ms delay between cycles. Check all pigpio initialization and I2C/SPI calls for errors, and handle sensor-absent and I2C bus-error paths gracefully. Use a SIGINT signal handler for clean resource release: turn off the LED strip, close all I2C handles, close the SPI handle, and terminate pigpio on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library for GPIO and the standard Linux i2c-dev interface for I2C (not wiringPi or any deprecated library) to control the brightness of a WS2812B LED strip based on readings from a VEML7700 ambient light sensor at I2C address 0x10. Initialize the VEML7700 with configuration register 0x00 set to 0x0000 (integration time 100 ms, gain 1/8) and read the ALS data from register 0x04 (16-bit). Convert the raw value to lux using lux = raw * 0.0036 * (1/gain) * (100ms/integration_time), which for the default settings reduces to lux = raw * 0.0288. Map the lux value (range 0 to 120000) to LED brightness (0-255) using gamma correction: brightness = 255 * pow(lux / 120000.0, 1.0/2.2). Drive the WS2812B strip via a single GPIO18 pin, bit-banging with libgpiod: toggle the pin at a high frequency such as 800 kHz with duty cycle proportional to brightness, or fall back to threshold-based on/off control if bit-banging is not feasible. Gracefully handle I2C errors, such as sensor absence or bus errors, by retrying up to 3 times with a 100 ms delay between retries, then logging an error and continuing. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to cleanly release GPIO lines, close I2C file descriptors, and turn off the LED strip. Run in an infinite loop with a 200 ms delay between iterations, printing the current lux and brightness values to stdout.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (gpiod_line_* functions; no sysfs, no wiringPi, no pigpio) to interface with a KY-026 flame sensor (digital output, active-low) on GPIO4. Upon flame detection (sensor output LOW), activate a buzzer on GPIO17 and an LED on GPIO18. On startup, run a self-test: blink the LED twice (500 ms on, 500 ms off) with the buzzer off, then read the flame sensor 5 times at 100 ms intervals; if it consistently reads LOW (flame detected) all 5 times, treat it as a sensor fault. On self-test failure, signal the error with a distinct pattern -- the LED blinking rapidly (100 ms on/off) for 5 cycles, then the buzzer sounding a short-short-long-short pattern (200 ms, 200 ms, 600 ms, 200 ms) repeated 3 times -- then exit with code 1. After self-test passes, poll the flame sensor every 50 ms in the main loop; when flame is detected (LOW), activate the buzzer and LED continuously until the sensor reads HIGH for at least one sample, then deactivate them. Log all events (flame detected, flame gone, errors) with timestamps. Check every gpiod call, including line requests and value reads/writes, and handle failures gracefully with clear error messages. Clean up all GPIO lines on normal exit and on SIGINT (Ctrl+C) using a signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Linux i2c-dev interface (not sysfs) to read ambient light from a BH1750 digital light sensor at I2C address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1, initialized in continuous high-resolution mode (command 0x10). Read the 2-byte raw value every 1 second and convert it to lux using lux = raw / 1.2. Store the last 60 lux readings in a circular buffer and compute the average lux over the buffer. Control an LED on GPIO17 (BCM numbering) via sysfs GPIO, blinking it at a rate proportional to the average lux, from 0.5 Hz (dark) to 5 Hz (bright, 1000+ lux), using the linear mapping rate = 0.5 + (avg_lux / 1000) * 4.5, clamped to [0.5, 5.0]. The blink pattern is a 50% duty cycle square wave (on for half period, off for half period). If an I2C read fails, print an error, skip that sample, and retry on the next loop iteration. On program exit (Ctrl+C), cleanly release the GPIO (unexport) and close the I2C file descriptor, using signal(SIGINT) for graceful shutdown. Use only standard POSIX and Linux kernel headers, no external libraries beyond those.
