prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not wiringPi or pigpio) to control a common-cathode RGB LED by randomly changing its color every 100 ms, using software PWM via a simple timing loop (no hardware PWM). Wire Red to GPIO24 (physical pin 18), Green to GPIO23 (physical pin 16), and Blue to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) (BCM numbering). Drive each channel with a 100 Hz PWM signal (10 ms period) with a duty cycle from 0 to 100. Initialize all three GPIOs as outputs; generate random RGB values (0-100) using rand() seeded with time(NULL) and set the PWM duty cycles accordingly. Use gpiod_line_set_value() in a busy-wait PWM loop, avoiding sleep calls shorter than 1 ms and using clock_nanosleep for precision. Check gpiod_chip_open_by_number(), gpiod_chip_get_line(), and gpiod_line_request_output() for each line, handling failures with descriptive messages. Run indefinitely until Ctrl+C, which should cleanly release GPIO lines via a SIGINT signal handler and exit, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO to interface with an Adafruit LSM303DLHC accelerometer at I2C address 0x19 on bus 1, detecting sudden impacts exceeding a configurable G-force threshold (default 2.0G, set via a -t command-line argument). Configure the sensor with CTRL_REG1_A=0x27 (enable all axes, 100 Hz) and CTRL_REG4_A=0x00 (2G full-scale, sensitivity 16384 LSB/G), and use multi-byte reads with the auto-increment bit (0x80) starting at OUT_X_L_A (0x28). Continuously poll the accelerometer at 10 Hz, calculate the total G-force magnitude, and when the threshold is exceeded, pulse GPIO17 (set as output) HIGH for 50 ms and log timestamped accelerometer data to 'impact_log.txt'. Check every I2C read/write, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release (I2C handle, GPIO, pigpio library) on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with an Analog Devices ADPD188BI optical sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x39. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x01 to register 0x0D (MODE) to enter normal operation mode. Read ambient light (ALS) data from 16-bit registers 0x64 (LSB) and 0x65 (MSB), combining them into a 16-bit unsigned value, and read color (RGB) data from 16-bit registers 0x66 (Red), 0x68 (Green), and 0x6A (Blue). Log each timestamped reading (ALS, R, G, B) to a CSV file named 'color_log.csv' with a header row. Simulate a smart lighting system by adjusting LED brightness on GPIO18 (hardware PWM) using pigpio: map the ALS value (0-65535) to a PWM duty cycle (0-255), so brighter ambient light increases LED brightness. Handle I2C errors, such as failed writes/reads or sensor absence, by logging to stderr and retrying after 100 ms. Use signal handling (SIGINT/SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, turning off the LED, and closing the CSV file. Sample every 500 ms.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses pigpio for I2C (never wiringPi) to interface with an Adafruit FXOS8700CQ 6-axis accelerometer/magnetometer at I2C address 0x1F on bus 1, detecting sudden impacts by computing the acceleration magnitude. On startup, verify the sensor by reading WHO_AM_I (register 0x0D) and checking it equals 0xC7, aborting with a clear error if it does not match. Initialize the sensor: place it into standby (clear CTRL_REG1 bit 0), configure XYZ_DATA_CFG (0x0E) for ±2g mode (0x00), then activate by setting CTRL_REG1 (0x2A) bit 0 (active mode, 200 Hz ODR). Read 6 bytes of acceleration starting at OUT_X_MSB (0x01); the data is 14-bit left-justified, so shift right by 2, then convert using sensitivity 4096 counts/g for the ±2g range and multiply by 9.81 for m/s^2. Compute magnitude = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2); if it exceeds the 2g (19.62 m/s^2) threshold, log the timestamp, x, y, z, and magnitude to 'impact_log.txt' in append mode as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,x,y,z,magnitude' with 3 decimal places. Sample every 50 ms. Check every pigpio I2C call's return value; on a read error, print a diagnostic to stderr and continue the loop rather than crashing. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT (Ctrl+C): close the I2C handle, call gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface (/dev/i2c-1 character device) to read angular velocity from a GY-50 L3G4200D gyroscope at I2C address 0x69 (SA0 tied high) on bus 1. Configure CTRL_REG1 (0x20) to 0x0F (normal mode, all axes enabled, 100 Hz ODR) and CTRL_REG4 (0x23) to 0x00 (250 dps full-scale, continuous update). Read the 6-byte OUT_X_L..OUT_Z_H block starting at register 0x28 using an auto-increment read, and convert the raw 16-bit signed values to degrees per second using a sensitivity of 0.00875 dps/LSB. Perform a 100-sample stationary calibration at startup to compute X/Y/Z zero-rate offsets. Log the calibrated X, Y, Z readings with ISO-8601 timestamps to 'gyro_log.txt' at 20 Hz (50 ms period). If any axis exceeds 50 dps, print a warning to stderr and append an alert line to the log. Check every open, ioctl, read, and write call; detect sensor absence via WHO_AM_I (register 0x0F, expected 0xD3) and handle I2C bus errors. Cleanly release the I2C file descriptor and log file on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read acceleration data from an ADXL345 accelerometer over I2C bus 1 at address 0x53. Configure the sensor for full-resolution, ±2g range, and verify the DEVID register (0x00) reads 0xE5 before proceeding. Read the 6 bytes of X/Y/Z data starting at register 0x32 every 100 ms (10 Hz). Log each sample to 'accel_log.txt' as 'timestamp,x,y,z' in g units with 3 decimal places. Turn on an LED connected to GPIO17 (active-high) when the absolute acceleration on ANY axis exceeds 2.0 g, otherwise turn it off. Check every pigpio/I2C call, and handle I2C read failures without writing garbage to the log. Ensure clean resource release (I2C handle, GPIO, log file) on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses pigpio for I2C to read magnetometer and accelerometer data from a GY-51 LSM303DLHC over I2C bus 1 (accelerometer address 0x19, magnetometer address 0x1E) and calculate a tilt-compensated heading. Initialize the accelerometer with CTRL_REG1_A (0x20) set to 0x27 (50 Hz, all axes enabled) and the magnetometer with MR_REG_M (0x02) set to 0x00 (continuous-conversion mode). Read 6 bytes from each sensor: accelerometer data from OUT_X_L_A (0x28) with the auto-increment bit, and magnetometer data from OUT_X_H_M (0x03). Log timestamped heading, acceleration (x, y, z in g), and magnetic field (x, y, z in gauss) to 'compass_log.txt', writing a CSV header if the log file is new. Check every I2C call and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Sample every 100 ms. Use SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handles and terminates pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses pigpio to continuously read distance from an Adafruit VL6180X Time-of-Flight sensor via I2C bus 1 at address 0x29, simulating a proximity-based automated door opener. Perform the VL6180X's mandatory initialization sequence before use (read register 0x016, write 0x0207 to register 0x000, and the remaining sequence steps). Sample every 100 ms, reading the range status register (0x04d) to detect errors such as overrange or signal failure. If the measured distance is less than 100 mm, log 'DOOR_OPEN'; otherwise log 'DOOR_CLOSED'. Log timestamped readings to 'distance_log.txt'. Check all I2C read/write return values and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths by attempting re-initialization. Handle SIGINT for clean resource release.

prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio to sample data from two STMicroelectronics IMP23ABSU ultrasonic MEMS microphone sensors on I2C bus 1, simulating a bat echolocation analysis system. The two sensors have distinct I2C addresses: sensor 1 at 0x68 and sensor 2 at 0x69, each exposing a 16-bit data register at 0x01 and a control register at 0x00 that must be written with 0x80 to enable continuous measurement. Read 16-bit signed audio samples from both sensors, timestamp them using CLOCK_REALTIME, compute a basic Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) by subtracting the two samples, and log the data as CSV to 'audio_log.dat' with columns sec, nsec, sensor1, sensor2, tdoa. Use a 10 ms sampling interval. Verify all pigpio initialization and I2C communication calls; handle sensor-absent or bus-failure paths gracefully by skipping the sample and retrying. Ensure clean resource release (I2C handles, log file, pigpio termination) on all exit paths via a SIGINT signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface over SPI with an Analog Devices ADIS16488A IMU on SPI channel 0 (CE0 on GPIO8) at 1 MHz, SPI mode 3 (CPOL=1, CPHA=1), using pigpio SPI flags 0b11000000000 (bit 9 = CPHA, bit 10 = CPOL, bit 8 = aux SPI off) and 16-bit words. The ADIS16488A read protocol sends a 16-bit word whose MSB is 0 followed by the 7-bit register address; the requested register's data is returned on the next 16-bit transfer, so implement a dummy read or stall of at least 40 microseconds between the request and the data-retrieval transfer. Continuously read gyroscope X, Y, Z from registers X_GYRO=0x04, Y_GYRO=0x06, Z_GYRO=0x08 and accelerometer X, Y, Z from X_ACCEL=0x0A, Y_ACCEL=0x0C, Z_ACCEL=0x0E every 100 ms, converting with sensitivities 0.005 deg/sec/LSB for gyroscope and 0.00025 g/LSB for accelerometer, and log each sample with a millisecond-precision timestamp to a CSV file named "imu_data.csv" whose header row is "timestamp,gyro_x,gyro_y,gyro_z,accel_x,accel_y,accel_z". Check the return values of gpioInitialise, spiOpen and fopen; if spiXfer returns less than 0, log the error to stderr and skip that sample rather than aborting. Use a non-blocking sampling delay that checks a running flag every few milliseconds so the program responds promptly to signals, and implement a cleanup() helper registered with atexit() that closes the SPI handle and CSV file and terminates pigpio on SIGINT, SIGTERM and every other exit path.
raw:
```
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -std=c11 -o imu_data imu_data.c -lpigpio
$ ./imu_data
```

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with an Analog Devices ADIS16448 IMU over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8) at 1 MHz, SPI Mode 0. The ADIS16448 requires a two-cycle SPI read: send the read command (register address with bit 15 set) in the first 16-bit transfer, wait at least 40 microseconds of stall time, then send a dummy 0x0000 in the second transfer to clock out the 16-bit data. Periodically read gyroscope x, y, z from X_GYRO_OUT=0x04, Y_GYRO_OUT=0x06, Z_GYRO_OUT=0x08 and accelerometer x, y, z from X_ACCL_OUT=0x0A, Y_ACCL_OUT=0x0C, Z_ACCL_OUT=0x0E, scaling with 0.05 deg/sec/LSB for gyroscope and 0.00025 g/LSB for accelerometer, and print the formatted values to the console every 100 ms. Include robust error handling for pigpio initialization, SPI open, and transfer failures, and handle Ctrl+C cleanly by closing the SPI handle and calling gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TDK MPU-6886 6-axis IMU over I2C bus 1 at address 0x68 using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open/ioctl/read/write), not wiringPi. Verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x75) and checking it returns 0x86, then initialize the sensor by waking it (PWR_MGMT_1 = 0x00) and setting ACCEL_CONFIG (0x1C) and GYRO_CONFIG (0x1B) to 0x00 for the +-2g and +-250 dps ranges. Every 50 ms, read raw accelerometer data from registers 0x3B-0x40 and gyroscope data from registers 0x43-0x48, and print the raw 16-bit signed values to the console. Check every I2C syscall, retry transient read failures up to 3 times, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths gracefully, ensuring clean resource release by closing the I2C file descriptor on all exit paths including SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library for I2C and GPIO to interface with an Adafruit ADXL345 accelerometer on I2C bus 1 at address 0x53, configured for full-resolution mode at the +-2g range (scale factor 256 LSB/g), to detect sudden impacts. Verify the ADXL345 device ID by reading register 0x00 and checking it equals 0xE5. Poll the sensor every 10 ms; if the total acceleration magnitude exceeds 2.5g, turn on a red LED connected to GPIO17 for 500 ms and append a timestamped entry containing the magnitude and X/Y/Z components to "impact_log.txt". Check every I2C read/write call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, LED, log file, and pigpio on all exit paths including SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library for all I2C operations to read accelerometer and gyroscope data from a TDK InvenSense ICM-20602 IMU on I2C bus 1 at address 0x68. Initialize the device by waking it from sleep (PWR_MGMT_1 = 0x00), setting the accelerometer to +-2g (ACCEL_CONFIG = 0x00) and the gyroscope to +-250 dps (GYRO_CONFIG = 0x00), and before the main loop verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x75) and checking for the expected value 0x12. Use burst reads (i2cReadI2CBlockData) to fetch the 6 accelerometer bytes starting at 0x3B and the 6 gyroscope bytes starting at 0x43 efficiently, and log timestamped raw x, y, z accelerometer and gyroscope values to a CSV file named 'imu_log.csv' at 10 Hz (100 ms interval). Check the return value of every I2C operation and print failures to stderr, and handle Ctrl+C (SIGINT) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the CSV file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads X, Y, and Z acceleration data from a GY-45 MMA8451Q accelerometer over I2C bus 1 at address 0x1D, using the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface for I2C access (libgpiod has no I2C API) and libgpiod for the LED GPIO line on GPIO17 (BCM numbering) — never wiringPi. Verify the sensor's identity by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x0D) and checking it equals 0x1A before operation. Poll the sensor every 100 ms and trigger the LED if the magnitude of acceleration on any axis exceeds a threshold of 2.0g, given the sensor's default +-2g range where 1g = 1024 counts; when an impact is detected, turn the LED on for 500 ms and append a timestamped entry to 'impact_log.txt'. Handle I2C read/write errors gracefully, and cleanly release all resources — the I2C bus, GPIO lines, and file handles — on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads X, Y, and Z magnetic field data from a Texas Instruments TMAG5273 I2C 3D Hall-Effect sensor at its default address 0x35, using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface directly (open/ioctl/read/write) rather than wiringPi, to simulate an industrial robotic arm joint position feedback system. Use 16-bit little-endian reads for the X, Y, and Z result registers at 0x10, 0x11, and 0x12, sampling once per second, and log the data with timestamps to 'magnetic_field_log.csv', writing the CSV header row on startup if the file does not already exist. Check every syscall (open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, etc.) and handle errors gracefully; if an I2C read fails, log an error to stderr and continue the loop. Implement a signal handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM that cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file.

Read all 6 data bytes starting at OUT_X_L (0x28) in a single block read, and convert raw values to degrees per second using sensitivity 8.75 mdps/LSB (i.e., divide by 114.285). Log each sample with a nanosecond-precision timestamp to 'gyro_log.csv' with a header row 'Timestamp,X,Y,Z', sampling every 10 ms. Retry I2C writes up to 3 times during initialization, check every I2C call, verify the WHO_AM_I register (0x0F) reads 0xD3 before proceeding, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Use signal handling for graceful termination, performing clean resource release on SIGINT by closing the I2C handle, closing the file, and calling gpioTerminate().

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8), 1 MHz clock, SPI Mode 0, to read acceleration data from an Analog Devices ADXL354B accelerometer. The ADXL354B outputs 20-bit signed acceleration data in 3 consecutive bytes per axis (XDATA at 0x08, YDATA at 0x0B, ZDATA at 0x0E); use the +-2g range sensitivity of 3.9 microg/LSB (0.0000039 g/LSB). SPI reads use bit 7 = 1 for read and bit 6 = 1 for multi-byte. Implement a proper device reset sequence: write 0x52 to the RESET register (0x1F), wait 1 ms, then set the measurement mode by clearing the RUN bit in POWER_CTL (0x2D), waiting for the STABLE bit in STATUS (0x04), then setting the RUN bit. Log X, Y, and Z axis readings with timestamps every 100 ms to a file named 'vibration_log.txt'. Handle SPI communication errors with retries, check sensor presence by reading PARTID (0x01, expected 0x1D), and implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT/SIGTERM with proper resource cleanup: close the SPI handle, close the file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library's spiOpen and spiXfer APIs (not deprecated wiringPi) to interface with an Analog Devices ADIS16362 IMU over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8), baud rate 1 MHz, SPI Mode 3 (active-high clock, sampled on trailing edge). The ADIS16362 read protocol sends the register address with the MSB set followed by a dummy byte, with the requested register's data returned on the next 16-bit transfer; implement a robust read function that sends the address, waits for the conversion, and retrieves the data, handling stall/error returns from spiXfer. Continuously read 3-axis gyroscope from X_GYRO=0x04, Y_GYRO=0x06, Z_GYRO=0x08 and 3-axis accelerometer from X_ACCL=0x0A, Y_ACCL=0x0C, Z_ACCL=0x0E, scaling with 0.05 deg/sec/LSB for gyroscope and 0.0025 g/LSB for accelerometer, sampling at approximately 100 Hz (10 ms delay between reads). Log timestamped readings to a comma-separated file 'imu_log.csv' starting with the header 'Timestamp,X_Gyro,Y_Gyro,Z_Gyro,X_Accel,Y_Accel,Z_Accel', using high-precision UNIX epoch timestamps (seconds.nanoseconds). Check pigpio initialization, SPI open, file open, and spiXfer return codes; if spiXfer fails, print an error to stderr and skip the logging iteration. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT (Ctrl+C) using a signal handler that safely closes the SPI handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not the deprecated sysfs interface, and not wiringPi) to read an E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensor connected to GPIO17. The E18-D80NK outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected within its detection range, adjustable up to about 80 cm and configured here for roughly 30 cm, and HIGH (1) when the path is clear. Open the gpiochip device for GPIO17 on the Raspberry Pi 5 (gpiochip4) and request the line for input direction using modern libgpiod APIs such as gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_line_open, gpiod_line_request_input, and gpiod_line_get_value. Poll the sensor every 1 second; when an obstacle is detected (line reads LOW), trigger a simulated "self-parking" sequence logged to the console with timestamps ("Self-parking sequence started" / "completed"). Check all libgpiod calls, handle the case where the gpiochip or line is unavailable and exit gracefully, and handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for clean shutdown, releasing the GPIO line and closing the chip on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses libgpiod (v2 API) to interface with two Keyes KY-032 IR obstacle avoidance sensors connected to GPIO17 and GPIO27 (physical pins 11 and 13, BCM numbering). The KY-032 output is active-low: the sensor reads 0 when an obstacle is detected and 1 when the path is clear. Use a single gpiochip and request both lines together for input, reading both lines in a single call via the libgpiod v2 bulk-read API gpiod_line_request_get_values. Poll both sensors every 100 ms and log the obstacle detection status to the console with a timestamp, simulating a basic collision avoidance system for a small robot, running in an infinite loop until interrupted. Check every libgpiod call, handle the case where the gpiochip or lines are unavailable, and ensure clean release of all resources on all exit paths including SIGINT (Ctrl+C). Compile cleanly with -Wall -Wextra against libgpiod >= 2.0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the modern libgpiod library for SPI chip-select line control together with the Linux spidev interface for SPI communication (not the deprecated bcm2835 or wiringPi libraries) to periodically read gyroscope data from an Analog Devices ADIS16266 connected on SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8), configured for SPI Mode 3, MSB first, at a 1 MHz clock speed. Initialize the SPI device (/dev/spidev0.0) and a libgpiod line for the CS pin, write to the MSC_CTRL register (0x24) to enable data ready mode, then periodically read the X, Y, and Z angular rate output registers (0x04, 0x06, 0x08) using the ADIS16266 two-transfer read protocol (send the address with the MSB set, then read 2 bytes). Convert the raw 16-bit signed values to angular rates using the scale factor of 0.02 deg/sec/LSB and log the results to the console every 100 ms. Include robust error handling: check all SPI and GPIO initialization calls, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT, running in a loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses only the pigpio C API, not wiringPi, to read accelerometer and gyroscope data from an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR connected via I2C bus 1 at the 7-bit address 0x6B. Initialize the pigpio library and open the I2C bus, then verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register and checking it returns 0x6B. Configure the accelerometer for +-2g full-scale at 104 Hz (CTRL1_XL = 0x42) and the gyroscope for +-250 dps at 104 Hz (CTRL2_G = 0x42). Every 100 ms, burst-read 12 bytes starting at OUTX_L_G (0x22) covering gyro X/Y/Z then accel X/Y/Z, convert to physical units using gyro sensitivity mdps/LSB = 8.75 (i.e. 0.00875 dps/LSB) and accel sensitivity mg/LSB = 0.061 (i.e. 0.000061 g/LSB), and print one line to stdout. Handle all error paths: pigpio init failure, I2C open failure, WHO_AM_I mismatch, register write failures, and short or failed burst reads, printing to stderr and exiting non-zero; check every I2C call's return value and never use hard-coded sleeps that ignore errors. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C triggers a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read accelerometer and magnetometer data from an Adafruit FXOS8700 breakout board over I2C at address 0x1D on bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3 for SDA/SCL). Initialize the sensor into hybrid mode by configuring CTRL_REG1 (0x2A), CTRL_REG2 (0x2B), M_CTRL_REG1 (0x5B), and M_CTRL_REG2 (0x5C) so both the accelerometer and magnetometer produce data. Every 100 ms, read the 12-byte combined data block starting at register 0x01 (OUT_X_MSB), which contains 6 bytes of 14-bit left-aligned accelerometer data followed by 6 bytes of 16-bit magnetometer data, and log the raw X, Y, and Z values for both sensors to the console each cycle. Handle I2C communication errors robustly: check every pigpio I2C call, verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x0D, expected value 0xC7) before initialization, and retry on transient read failures. Clean up all resources — close the I2C handle and terminate pigpio — on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that interfaces with an ADXL345 accelerometer over I2C at address 0x53 using the Linux i2c-dev interface via /dev/i2c-1, not wiringPi, since libgpiod itself has no I2C API. Read X, Y, Z data from registers 0x32-0x37, calculate tilt angles using atan2, and log events with timestamps every 100 ms. Log tilt events exceeding a threshold of 30.0 degrees to '/var/log/tilt_events.log'. Include robust error handling for I2C communication failures, explicitly handling sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for Ctrl+C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library, and no wiringPi, to monitor ambient noise levels via a KY-038 sound sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11). The KY-038 OUT pin is active-high and pulses when sound exceeds its onboard comparator threshold. Accept a single command-line argument — an integer threshold representing the minimum number of high-readings per 5-second window required to trigger an alert — and validate it, rejecting non-numeric or non-positive values. Continuously sample GPIO17 every 1 ms for 5 seconds, counting how many times the pin reads high; at the end of each 5-second window, print a timestamped ALERT to stdout if the high-reading count exceeds the threshold, otherwise print a normal status line. Run in a continuous loop until signaled to stop, with a 1-second pause between monitoring windows. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully, terminating pigpio and exiting cleanly, and check every pigpio call for failure (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode), printing clear error messages to stderr on any failure.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod C API, never wiringPi, to control two 12V electromagnetic door locks actuated by 5V active-HIGH relay modules driven via TIP120 transistors on GPIO17 (Door A) and GPIO27 (Door B), based on a randomly generated 6-digit security code. Initialize GPIO17 and GPIO27 as outputs, both defaulting to LOW (locks energized/closed); a HIGH signal de-energizes the relay and unlocks the corresponding door. Generate a random 6-digit code between 100000 and 999999 at startup and print it to stdout. In a loop, prompt the user to enter the code via stdin; if it matches, unlock Door A (GPIO17 HIGH) for 5 seconds, then re-lock it (LOW), log the successful entry to 'access_log.txt' as a CSV row 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,NNNNNN', and generate a new random code. If the code does not match, print 'Access denied' and continue; handle invalid non-numeric stdin input gracefully by clearing the buffer and re-prompting. Check every libgpiod call (chip open, line get, line request) and file open, printing meaningful errors to stderr and exiting non-zero on initialization failure. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop exits cleanly; on exit, drive both GPIO outputs LOW (locked), release all libgpiod resources (lines and chip), and close any open file handles. Compile with: gcc -Wall -o door_access door_access.c -lgpiod.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the standard Linux /dev/i2c-1 ioctl interface, not the unmaintained bcm2835 library, to read illuminance from a BH1750FVI light sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3). The sensor's ADDR pin is tied to GND, so the I2C address is 0x23. Write the One-Time High-Resolution Mode 2 command (0x21) to the sensor, wait for the maximum conversion time of 180 ms, then read 2 bytes of data and calculate the illuminance in lux using the formula: (raw_value * 5) / 6 (equivalent to raw_value / 1.2). prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio for I2C and hardware PWM to implement a theremin using an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A. The program acts as a TCP server listening on port 12345; when a client sends a message starting with 'MOTION_DETECTED:' and containing the shared secret 'MySecretKey', the theremin plays tones for 5 seconds based on capacitive touch readings, using hardware PWM on GPIO18. Initialize the MPR121 with proper soft-reset and electrode configuration, and map the maximum electrode filtered data value to a frequency in the range 220-880 Hz using a logarithmic scale, sampling touch values every 20 ms during the 5-second playback window and logging each frequency to 'frequency_log.txt'. Handle errors for pigpio initialization, I2C open/read, and socket/bind/listen/accept. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, stop PWM, close I2C and sockets, and terminate pigpio cleanly.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with an LSM303DLHC magnetometer via I2C bus 1 at default address 0x1E, connected to the physical SDA1/SCL1 pins, and controls an LED on GPIO17. Use libgpiod for GPIO/PWM control and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1, ioctl) for sensor communication, not wiringPi. Initialize the magnetometer by writing 0x18 to CTRL_REG1_M (0x20) for 10 Hz continuous conversion, and read 6 bytes of data starting from OUT_X_L_M (0x08) in a single I2C block read. The program must read X, Y, Z magnetic field data, compute the magnitude of the Z-axis field, and adjust the LED brightness proportionally using hardware PWM, sampling every 100 ms in the main loop. Handle I2C errors (e.g., sensor absent, bus errors) gracefully by logging the error and skipping the sample without crashing, and implement clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM by releasing the PWM, closing the I2C file descriptor, and closing any log files.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with an HMC5883L magnetometer via I2C on bus 1 at address 0x1E. Configure the sensor for 8-sample averaging, 15 Hz output rate, and a gain setting of 1.3 Gauss (Configuration Register A = 0x70, Configuration Register B = 0x20, Mode register = 0x00 for continuous mode). Continuously collect raw readings to compute hard-iron offsets as a running average over a 100-sample window. Every 500 ms, apply the current hard-iron offsets to the latest raw reading and print the offset-corrected (not unit-normalized) X, Y, and Z values to stdout. Explicitly flag any I2C read/write errors on stderr without crashing, and ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle and pigpio library on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use FIFOs or secondary processes.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads tri-axial acceleration data from an LSM303D accelerometer/magnetometer connected via I2C at address 0x1D (SA0 tied high) on /dev/i2c-1, using the Linux i2c-dev kernel API (open, ioctl I2C_SLAVE, i2c_smbus_read_byte_data, i2c_smbus_write_byte_data, i2c_smbus_read_i2c_block_data) for I2C communication, not wiringPi, and the libgpiod library for the GPIO interrupt line request and event monitoring, not wiringPiISR. The LSM303D's INT1 pin is connected to GPIO23 (BCM pin 23, physical pin 16). Verify the WHO_AM_I register (0x0F) reads 0x49 before proceeding, then configure the accelerometer for 50 Hz ODR with all axes enabled (CTRL_REG1 = 0x57), full-scale +-2g (CTRL_REG4 = 0x00, sensitivity 0.061 mg/LSB), and a threshold interrupt on any-axis-high event (INT1_CFG = 0x2A) with threshold 2000 mg (register value = 2000/16 = 125 = 0x7D) and duration 0 (immediate). Use a 6-byte multi-byte burst read from OUT_X_L_A (0x28) with auto-increment (MSB of the register address set to 0x80). Poll acceleration at roughly 10 ms intervals and store each sample in a 64-entry in-memory circular buffer; on a rising edge of the INT1 GPIO interrupt, print a timestamp and dump the last 10 buffered samples. Check every I2C read/write and file-open call, printing a diagnostic to stderr and exiting non-zero on initialization failure; if a runtime I2C read fails, print a warning to stderr and skip that sample without corrupting the buffer. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl-C) gracefully by disabling the accelerometer (CTRL_REG1 = 0x00), closing the I2C file descriptor, and exiting cleanly. Compile with: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o lsm303d_mon lsm303d_mon.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library, never wiringPi, to actuate two 12V DC push-pull solenoids in an alternating sequence with a 500 ms delay between each transition, simulating a simple reciprocating linear actuator for a miniature automated assembly line prototype. Solenoid 1 is driven via a TIP120 transistor on GPIO17 (BCM numbering); solenoid 2 via a TIP120 transistor on GPIO27 (BCM numbering); both circuits include flyback diodes. Request the gpiochip and both lines with consumer labels, checking every libgpiod call for errors and printing a diagnostic to stderr on failure. Before entering the main loop, drive both lines LOW so no solenoid is energized at startup. In the loop, alternate: energize solenoid 1 for 500 ms, then de-energize solenoid 1 and energize solenoid 2 for 500 ms, then de-energize solenoid 2, using nanosleep for the timing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly releases both lines (sets them LOW) and frees all libgpiod resources before exiting.

Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM: ensure both locks are set to LOW (locked), close the serial handles, and call gpioTerminate().

Access I2C through ioctl and linux/i2c-dev.h, with exponential-backoff retries on sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Log timestamped, comma-separated pitch, roll, and servo position values to solar_tracker.log. Release all resources cleanly on every exit path via SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling. Do not use external networking or JSON libraries — limit the program to local sensor reading, PWM control, and file logging.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to control four relay-controlled lamp actuators on GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22, simulating a smart home lighting system with a sunrise/sunset effect driven by a 24-hour schedule read from lighting_schedule.txt (format HH:MM:SS,relay_number,on/off). Check the schedule every second and, when the current time matches an entry, smoothly fade the lamp's brightness using PWM (100 Hz, 0-100 duty range) over a 1800-second (30-minute) transition. Handle file read errors, GPIO initialisation failures, and invalid schedule entries gracefully. Use SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling to turn off all relays and release GPIO resources cleanly on exit, and avoid calling non-reentrant functions such as fopen and localtime inside the signal handler.

Linearly map distances from 2 cm to 30 cm to frequencies from 200 Hz to 2000 Hz, clamping the result to that range before applying it. Generate the 10 microsecond trigger pulse with gpioDelay and measure the echo pulse width with microsecond-precision gpioTick timing. Run the main loop at roughly 50 Hz with at least a 60 ms gap between measurements to avoid trigger/echo overlap. Handle pigpio initialisation and HC-SR04 read failures robustly, including sensor-absent and timeout paths, logging failures to stderr. On SIGINT, silence the buzzer and deinitialise pigpio before exiting.

#define BUZZER_PIN 18
#define MIN_FREQ 200
#define MAX_FREQ 2000
#define MIN_DIST 2
#define MAX_DIST 30
#define MIN_US 10000
#define MAX_US 1000000
#define MIN_GAP 60000
#define MAX_GAP 1000000

static volatile int running = 1;

void handle_sigint(int sig) {
    running = 0;
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "pigpio initialisation failed\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (gpioSetMode(TRIGGER_PIN, PI_OUTPUT) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "failed to set trigger pin mode\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (gpioSetMode(ECHO_PIN, PI_INPUT) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "failed to set echo pin mode\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (gpioSetMode(BUZZER_PIN, PI_OUTPUT) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "failed to set buzzer pin mode\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (gpioSetPullUpDown(TRIGGER_PIN, PI_PUD_DOWN) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "failed to set trigger pin pull-up/down\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (gpioSetPullUpDown(ECHO_PIN, PI_PUD_DOWN) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "failed to set echo pin pull-up/down\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (gpioSetPullUpDown(BUZZER_PIN, PI_PUD_DOWN) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "failed to set buzzer pin pull-up/down\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    if (gpioSetAlertFunc(ECHO_PIN, handle_sigint) < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "failed to set echo pin alert function\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    signal(SIGINT, handle_sigint);

    while (running) {
        gpioWrite(TRIGGER_PIN, 1);
        usleep(MIN_US);
        gpioWrite(TRIGGER_PIN, 0);

        uint64_t start = gpioTick();
        uint64_t end = gpioTick();

        while (gpioRead(ECHO_PIN) == 0) {
            start = gpioTick();
        }

        while (gpioRead(ECHO_PIN) == 1) {
            end = gpioTick();
        }

        uint64_t us = (end - start) / 1000;

        if (us < MIN_US || us > MAX_US) {
            fprintf(stderr, "echo pulse width out of range\n");
            continue;
        }

        uint64_t dist = us / 58;

        if (dist < MIN_DIST || dist > MAX_DIST) {
            fprintf(stderr, "distance out of range\n");
            continue;
        }

        uint64_t freq = (dist * 1000) / 2;

        if (freq < MIN_FREQ || freq > MAX_FREQ) {
            fprintf(stderr, "frequency out of range\n");
            continue;
        }

        gpioPWM(BUZZER_PIN, freq);

        usleep(MIN_GAP);
    }

    gpioPWM(BUZZER_PIN, 0);
    gpioTerminate();

    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod API (gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_event_wait, gpiod_line_event_read) to read an SW-420 vibration sensor's active-high digital output on GPIO17 (physical pin 11), rather than the deprecated sysfs /sys/class/gpio interface. Poll for both rising and falling edges, using a poll timeout in milliseconds taken as a single command-line argument (default 1000 ms if omitted). Log every edge event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the raw value (0 or 1) to vibration_events.log, opening the file once and flushing or fsyncing after each write rather than reopening it per event; handle file open/write errors gracefully without terminating. Implement a basic earthquake early-warning simulation: maintain a sliding window of the last 5 events, and if 3 or more of them read HIGH, print an EARTHQUAKE ALERT message with the timestamp to the console. Check every libgpiod call and syscall for errors, printing diagnostics to stderr. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop exits cleanly, releasing the line and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads calibrated magnetic-field data from an LSM303DLHC magnetometer over I2C and logs it to a CSV file named mag_log.csv, using the Linux I2C-dev interface (/dev/i2c-1, linux/i2c-dev.h, ioctl-based SMBus reads/writes) rather than wiringPi, which is deprecated and unmaintained. The magnetometer's 7-bit I2C address is 0x1E, with SDA on physical pin 3 (GPIO2) and SCL on physical pin 5 (GPIO3). Configure continuous-conversion mode by writing 0x00 to MR_REG_M (register 0x02), and optionally set the output data rate to 15 Hz by writing 0x14 to CRA_REG_M (register 0x00). Read the six data registers 0x03-0x08 (X MSB, X LSB, Z MSB, Z LSB, Y MSB, Y LSB) and assemble them into signed 16-bit X, Y, and Z values. Apply hard-iron calibration offsets X_OFFSET=10, Y_OFFSET=-5, Z_OFFSET=20 to produce calibrated float values, then compute the compass heading in degrees from the calibrated X and Y values using atan2f, normalized to 0-360 degrees, and map it to one of eight compass directions (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW), printing the direction and numeric heading to the console. Once per second, append a row to mag_log.csv with columns Timestamp, Calibrated X, Calibrated Y, Calibrated Z, Heading, writing a header row first if the file does not already exist. Check the return value of every open, ioctl, read, write, and fopen call; on an I2C read failure, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip that sample rather than crashing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file, freeing all resources on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 via a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4. The TTP223 outputs HIGH (3.3 V) on touch and LOW when released; configure GPIO4 with a pull-down resistor. Debounce touches in software with a minimum 200 ms gap between registered touches inside the ISR callback, and on each valid touch toggle the relay and append a JSON object to relay_log.json in the form {"timestamp":"<ISO 8601>","relay_state":"ON|OFF"}. Check every pigpio call for errors and abort cleanly if gpioInitialise() or gpioSetISRFunc() fails. On SIGINT, turn the relay OFF, append a final OFF entry to the log, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting. Do not use any deprecated library such as wiringPi.

On timeout or any libgpiod call failure, log "-1" to the file and print an error to stderr; also report GPIO initialisation failures to stderr. Open the log file once in append mode at startup and keep it open for the program's lifetime. Enforce a 60 ms minimum guard between measurements to avoid false echoes. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM by releasing all libgpiod resources and closing the log file. Assume the HC-SR04's 5 V echo output is reduced to 3.3 V by a voltage divider or level shifter before reaching the Pi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B implementing a proximity-based automated door system using a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29, with the pigpio library used for both I2C and GPIO control. Perform a software reset of the VL53L1X (register 0x0000 = 0x00), then initialise it by setting the ranging mode and starting continuous ranging (register 0x0080 = 0x01). Poll the sensor every 100 ms: check the interrupt status register 0x0044 for data readiness, then read the 16-bit distance result from registers 0x0096 (MSB) and 0x0097 (LSB). Log the current distance to stdout each cycle, and drive a relay on BCM GPIO18 HIGH to simulate opening the door when the distance is 50 cm or less, otherwise LOW. Check every pigpio and I2C return value, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and log all errors to stderr. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle, set the relay LOW, and terminate pigpio for a clean shutdown.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read X, Y, and Z axis angular rates from an MPU-9250 gyroscope over SPI, using the standard Linux spidev interface with libgpiod for chip-select control rather than the unmaintained bcm2835 library. Open /dev/spidev0.0 and configure SPI at 1 MHz, mode 0, 8 bits per word, MSB first. Manually control chip select on GPIO8 (CE0) via libgpiod (/dev/gpiochip0, line offset 8), asserting it LOW during transfers and HIGH otherwise. Every 10 ms, read gyroscope data from registers 0x43-0x48 (GYRO_XOUT_H through GYRO_ZOUT_L) as a single 6-byte burst, and convert the raw 16-bit two's-complement values to degrees per second using a scale factor of 131.0 for the ±250 dps range. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp including nanoseconds to gyro_log.txt in CSV format: timestamp,x_rate,y_rate,z_rate. Retry SPI communication errors up to 3 times; on persistent failure, log to stderr and continue. Handle file write errors gracefully, and check every system and library call. Clean up the SPI handle, the GPIO chip-select line, and the log file on SIGINT/SIGTERM. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read angular velocity from an InvenSense MPU-6050 gyroscope over SPI (SPI mode, not I2C), using the Linux spidev interface with libgpiod for manual chip-select control on GPIO8 (CE0) — not bcm2835, which is unmaintained, and not wiringPi. Configure SPI at approximately 3.9 MHz, mode 0, asserting the CE0 chip-select line via libgpiod for each transfer. Read gyroscope X, Y, and Z axis data from registers 0x43, 0x45, and 0x47 (high bytes) with auto-increment disabled, using single-byte reads, and convert the raw 16-bit two's-complement values to degrees per second using the 131.0 LSB/(deg/s) sensitivity factor. Store each reading, with its timestamp, in a 64-entry in-memory circular buffer. If any axis exceeds ±200 deg/s, blink an LED on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) with 500 ms on/off intervals. Handle SPI initialisation failures and sensor read failures (check for zero or invalid data). On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), print the entire circular buffer as CSV with columns Timestamp, X, Y, Z, then release the SPI handle and GPIO resources on every exit path. The program should simulate a basic stability monitoring system.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) — pigpio has no support for the Raspberry Pi 5's RP1 I/O controller, so the earlier Pi 4 Model B is used instead — to read tilt from an MPU-6050 accelerometer/gyroscope on I2C bus 1 at address 0x68. Wake the sensor by writing 0x00 to PWR_MGMT_1 (register 0x6B) and set the accelerometer full-scale range to ±2g by writing 0x00 to ACCEL_CONFIG (register 0x1C), verifying successful configuration. Every 100 ms, read the 6 bytes of raw accelerometer data from registers 0x3B-0x40, and compute roll = atan2(y, z) * 180/pi and pitch = atan2(-x, sqrt(y^2 + z^2)) * 180/pi. Turn on an LED on GPIO21 if the absolute roll exceeds 45 degrees or the absolute pitch exceeds 45 degrees, otherwise turn it off. Log each reading to tilt_log.txt in CSV format with a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), roll, and pitch, and print roll and pitch to the console each cycle. Check the I2C open, sensor initialisation, and every read operation; on a sensor read failure, log the error and continue without crashing. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), turn off the LED, close the I2C handle, and terminate pigpio, with signal handling and resource cleanup on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with a Si1145 optical biometric sensor (assumed register-compatible with the Si1182-A-GM) over I2C, using the Linux I2C-dev interface (/dev/i2c-1, ioctl, read/write) for the sensor and libgpiod (gpiod_line_set_value, etc.) for GPIO — not wiringPi and not pigpio. The sensor is at I2C address 0x5A (8-bit). Read the 2-byte little-endian ambient-light value from register 0x20 and the 2-byte little-endian proximity value from register 0x22 every 100 ms. Log each timestamped reading in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,AmbientLight:XXXX,Proximity:XXXX' to biometric_log.txt in append mode. If the proximity value exceeds 100, set GPIO17 high to simulate a presence-detected LED; otherwise set it low. Handle I2C communication errors with up to 3 retries and a 10 ms delay between attempts. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers for graceful cleanup: close the I2C file descriptor, close the log file, and turn off the LED.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library for SPI and GPIO (not wiringPi) to read angular rate data from an Analog Devices ADXRS290 dual-axis gyroscope on SPI channel 0 (CE0, GPIO8) at a 1 MHz clock, SPI mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0). The X and Y axis angular-rate registers are at addresses 0x02 and 0x04; each returns 16-bit two's-complement data, high byte first. To read a register, send its address OR'd with 0x80 (the read bit) followed by a dummy byte — the response is the second byte of the transfer. The sensitivity is 200 LSB/deg/s. Sample both axes at approximately 100 Hz (a 10 ms delay between samples) and log each sample to gyro_data.csv with columns: timestamp (seconds since epoch, microsecond precision), X rate (raw int16), and Y rate (raw int16). If a read fails, attempt to reinitialise SPI up to 3 times before exiting. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, spiOpen, spiXfer) and file operation for errors. Use a SIGINT handler to cleanly close SPI, flush and close the file, and terminate pigpio, releasing all resources on every exit path.

Register edge-triggered pigpio callbacks for both rising and falling edges on each sensor. When both sensors simultaneously read HIGH for a continuous duration of at least 500 milliseconds, trigger an alert by setting GPIO17 HIGH for 2 seconds, then LOW. Check pigpio initialisation, the log file open, and callback registration for errors. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers that close the log file, set the alert pin LOW, and terminate pigpio. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

The relay simulates a light switch: touching electrode 0 toggles it on or off. Initialise pigpio and set GPIO17 as output, default LOW. Open the I2C device at address 0x5A on bus 1 and configure the MPR121 by writing: reset (register 0x80 = 0x63), stop mode (0x5E = 0x00), enable electrode 0 (0x5D = 0x01), touch threshold (0x41 = 0x0A), release threshold (0x42 = 0x08), debounce (0x5B = 0x21), charge time (0x5C = 0x0D), and run mode (0x5E = 0x0D). prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to control two 12V push-pull solenoids connected through TIP120 Darlington transistors to GPIO17 and GPIO27, simulating a simple pneumatic dispensing system. Initialise pigpio, handling initialisation failure by printing an error and exiting, and configure GPIO17 and GPIO27 as outputs with error checking. On each dispense cycle, activate solenoid 1 for half of a 1000 ms total dispense duration, then activate solenoid 2 for the remaining half, then deactivate both, using gpioDelay() (microseconds) for timing; repeat the dispense every 5 seconds in a continuous loop. Log each dispense event, with timestamp, solenoid pins, and duration in milliseconds, to dispense_log.txt, handling file open failures. Each function should return 0 on success and non-zero on failure, with main checking every return value and printing error messages to stderr. Register a SIGINT handler to gracefully deactivate both solenoids, terminate pigpio, and exit on Ctrl+C. Compile with -lpigpio.

Develop a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that controls two DC motors via an L298N dual H-bridge using only the pigpio library (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioPWM, gpioWrite, gpioDelay, gpioTerminate — no wiringPi or other deprecated API). Motor A uses GPIO17 (forward) and GPIO18 (backward); Motor B uses GPIO22 (forward) and GPIO23 (backward); the L298N's enable pins ENA (GPIO24) and ENB (GPIO25) must be held HIGH to allow PWM control, with all motor speeds clamped to +/-255. Simulate a self-balancing robot: an internal PID controller (Kp=1.0, Ki=0.01, Kd=0.1) generates motor commands every 50 ms from a simulated tilt error (a random float between -10.0 and 10.0 degrees). Also simulate an ultrasonic distance sensor returning a random value between 2.0 and 400.0 cm; if the distance is below 20 cm, reverse both motors at 50% speed for obstacle avoidance. Handle pigpio initialisation failure by printing an error and returning 1; handle log file open failure by printing an error, terminating pigpio, and returning 1; on an invalid motor character, log the error and skip. On SIGINT, stop the motors, close the log file, and terminate pigpio gracefully. Log every control cycle to balance_log.txt with columns: timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), tilt_error, distance, motor_a_speed, and motor_b_speed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library (not wiringPi, which is deprecated) to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) using a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4 (physical pin 7), simulating a smart light switch: each touch toggles the relay on or off. The TTP223 outputs logic HIGH when touched; assume an external pull-down resistor, or configure the internal pull-down via pigpio. The relay is active-high, energized when GPIO17 is HIGH. Debounce each touch with a delay of at least 50 ms after detection. Check every pigpio initialisation call and GPIO operation, handling sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. The program should run indefinitely until terminated by Ctrl+C.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to implement a 'mood light' driven by ambient noise from ALSA audio capture. Drive a common-cathode RGB LED on GPIO17 (red), GPIO18 (green), and GPIO27 (blue), each with a current-limiting resistor, using pigpio software PWM (gpioPWM) for smooth color control. Configure ALSA to capture from the 'default' device at 8000 Hz, 16-bit signed little-endian, 1 channel, with a period size of 1024 frames. Continuously read samples, compute the RMS amplitude, and map it to RGB PWM values using a non-linear transition — cool colors for low amplitude, warm colors for high amplitude. Accept an optional command-line sensitivity-scaling argument (default 1.0, must be positive). Check every pigpio and ALSA call: recover from buffer overruns (EPIPE) with snd_pcm_prepare, and from a suspended state (ESTRPIPE) with snd_pcm_resume. Include a 10 ms delay between updates, print status messages to stdout and errors to stderr, and release all resources — pigpio, ALSA, and allocated memory — on exit via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers. Gate ALSA support behind an ALSA_AVAILABLE compile-time macro: when ALSA is unavailable, simulate the audio input with a sine-wave amplitude so the mood light still cycles through colors, and ensure all exit paths remain clean with no resource leaks in either mode.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that interfaces with a TCS34725 color sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x29, using the pigpio library for both I2C and timing (gpioDelay for the 500 ms interval), simulating a color-based sorting system. Initialise the sensor with power-on and RGBC enable (register 0x80 = 0x03) and set the integration time to 154 ms (register 0x81 = 0xD5). Every 500 ms, read the calibrated clear, red, green, and blue values from the data registers starting at 0x14 (clear low byte) through 0x1A (blue high byte). Log the Unix-epoch timestamp and the four C, R, G, B values as a comma-separated line to color_data.csv, writing a header row first. Check every I2C open, write, and read operation; on failure, print an error to stderr, set the sensor's values to 0 for that cycle, and continue without crashing. Register SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers to close the I2C handle, close the file, and terminate pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to implement a sunrise/sunset lighting simulator controlling four independent 5V relay modules connected to lamps. The relays are active-low and wired to physical pins 11, 13, 15, and 17 (BCM GPIO17, GPIO27, GPIO22, GPIO23). Cycle repeatedly and indefinitely through four phases: sunrise, a gradual brightness increase over 1 hour; daytime, full brightness for 6 hours; sunset, a gradual brightness decrease over 1 hour; and nighttime, off for 14.4 hours. Simulate brightness with PWM-like relay toggling rather than true PWM, using an increasing duty cycle during sunrise and a decreasing duty cycle during sunset, with all four lamps running the same phase simultaneously. Use only the libgpiod functions gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_line_get, gpiod_line_request_output, gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_release, and gpiod_chip_close. Handle initialization failures from gpiod_chip_open_by_name and gpiod_line_request_output with clear error messages and a graceful exit. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, turn off all relays and release GPIO resources cleanly.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read X, Y, and Z angular velocities from an MPU-6050 gyroscope over I2C bus 1 at address 0x68 (AD0 pin low), for a basic vibration monitoring system. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x00 to register 0x6B to wake it, 0x07 to register 0x19 to set the sample rate divider to 125 Hz, and 0x00 to register 0x1B to set the gyroscope full-scale range to ±250°/s. Read the raw signed 16-bit gyroscope values from registers 0x43-0x48 (X_H, X_L, Y_H, Y_L, Z_H, Z_L) using a combined I2C block read, and convert them to degrees per second using a sensitivity of 131.0 LSB/(°/s). Sample at 100 Hz (10 ms interval) and log each reading to gyro_log.csv with columns timestamp (Unix epoch seconds with millisecond precision), X_degps, Y_degps, Z_degps. On a read failure, attempt sensor re-initialization (re-wake and re-configure) up to 3 times before logging an error and continuing. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cWriteByteData, i2cReadI2CBlockData). Use a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to close the log file and release the I2C handle, and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to control four SainSmart 5V relay modules on BCM GPIO pins 4, 17, 27, and 22 for a simulated smart greenhouse irrigation system. Each relay corresponds to one irrigation zone, and a simulated moisture sensor using rand() % 101 produces readings from 0 to 100 every 5 seconds, with the random generator seeded from time(NULL). If a zone's reading is below 30, drive its relay LOW to activate it, since the relays are active-low; otherwise drive it HIGH to deactivate it. Append each sensor reading, relay state, and a timestamp to irrigation_log.txt. Check pigpio initialization, the log file open, and every GPIO operation. On SIGINT or any error, safely deactivate all relays (drive HIGH), close the log file, and terminate pigpio, installing the handler with signal().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read accelerometer data from an Analog Devices ADXL345 over I2C at address 0x53. Configure the sensor for ±2g range with full resolution by writing 0x0B to the DATA_FORMAT register (0x31), and enable measurement mode by writing 0x08 to the POWER_CTL register (0x2D). Every 100 ms, read 6 bytes starting from the DATAX0 register (0x32) for the X, Y, Z axis data, and convert the raw signed 16-bit values to g-force using a scale factor of 256 LSB/g. Detect a freefall event when all three axes have an absolute value below 0.2g for a continuous 0.5 seconds, confirmed by reading twice with a 0.5 second delay. On a confirmed freefall, drive GPIO27 high to simulate an alarm, hold it for 5 seconds, then set it low. Log each freefall event to freefall.log in CSV format with a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) and x, y, z values to 3 decimal places. Handle I2C errors by printing to stderr and continuing operation, checking every pigpio and I2C call. Use a SIGINT handler to close the I2C handle, set GPIO low, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an interrupt-driven HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, TRIG on GPIO4 and ECHO on GPIO18 (BCM numbering). Send a 10 µs trigger pulse every 200 ms and measure the echo pulse width using rising-edge and falling-edge interrupt callbacks, correctly handling wrap-around of the 32-bit tick counter, which wraps roughly every 71.6 minutes. If the echo pulse width exceeds 23200 µs (about 4 meters, the sensor's maximum range) or no echo arrives within 100 ms of the trigger, discard the reading. Log each valid distance measurement in centimeters with a nanosecond-precision timestamp to distance_log.txt in CSV format: timestamp_ns,distance_cm. Protect the shared pulse-timing variables, which are updated from interrupt context, with a mutex. Handle pigpio initialization failure, file open failure, invalid pulse widths, and sensor timeouts. Use a SIGINT handler to cancel callbacks, close the file, terminate pigpio, and destroy the mutex, and run the measurement loop indefinitely.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to read acceleration data from an Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer over I2C bus 1 at address 0x18, implementing a basic fall detection system that triggers a buzzer on GPIO17. Initialize pigpio and I2C with error checking, and configure the LIS3DH for a 100 Hz data rate and ±2g full scale by writing 0x77 to CTRL_REG1 and 0x00 to CTRL_REG4. Continuously read 16-bit signed acceleration values starting from register OUT_X_L (0x28), converting to g using a sensitivity of 16384 LSB/g. Detect freefall when the acceleration magnitude drops below 0.2g, then detect impact when it exceeds 1.5g; on impact, activate the buzzer for 1 second. Accept optional command-line freefall and impact thresholds. Handle I2C communication failures with up to 3 retries and perform graceful cleanup on SIGINT. Handle sensor absence and bus errors robustly, and ensure resources are released on every exit path.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read magnetic field data from a Silicon Labs Si7210 Hall effect sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x30, and trigger a relay on GPIO 17 (active high) when the field strength exceeds a 5.0 mT threshold, sampling every 100 ms. Perform a one-shot measurement by writing 0x01 to register 0xC1 to start a conversion, polling register 0xC1 until it reads 0x00, then reading 2 bytes from register 0xC0 (byte 0 LSB, byte 1 MSB) and combining them into a signed 16-bit value: field_raw = (msb << 8) | lsb. Convert to milliTesla units of 0.01 mT with field_mT_x100 = field_raw * 25 / 1000, and compare against threshold * 100. If register 0xC1 does not clear after 50 poll attempts, log a timeout error and skip the cycle. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cReadByte, i2cWriteByte, i2cReadByteData, i2cWriteByteData); if i2cOpen fails, log the error and exit, and on any read/write failure, log the error, deactivate the relay, and retry on the next cycle. Append timestamped entries in ISO 8601 format to magnetic_events.txt for every field reading, relay state change, and error. Install a SIGINT handler that closes the I2C handle, deactivates the relay, terminates pigpio, and logs the shutdown.

Accept the commands "ON" and "OFF", case-insensitive and ignoring trailing whitespace, to control the relay. Log every activation, deactivation, and invalid-command event with a timestamp to relay_log.txt. Implement comprehensive error handling for socket operations (socket creation, bind, listen, accept, read) and for GPIO initialization. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM so the server shuts down gracefully: close all sockets, close the log file, turn off the relay, and terminate pigpio, ensuring clean resource release on every exit path.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read ambient light levels from a BH1750 sensor at I2C address 0x23 on I2C1 (GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL). Trigger a relay on GPIO23 to activate a grow light when the lux reading falls below 150, and deactivate it when lux is 150 or above. Use the BH1750 One-Time High-Resolution mode (command 0x20) and wait at least 120 ms for the conversion before reading the 2-byte result, converting to lux with lux = raw / 1.2. Log timestamps and lux values to grow_log.txt, sampling every 2 seconds. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures by checking the return codes of i2cOpen, i2cWriteByte, i2cReadDevice, and file operations, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging errors and retrying on the next cycle. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths — close the I2C handle, close the log file, deactivate the relay, and call gpioTerminate — with SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library, not wiringPi, to read weight from a TAL220B load cell via an HX711 amplifier, with DOUT on GPIO23 (physical pin 16) and SCK on GPIO24 (physical pin 18), and to trigger a solenoid lock on GPIO25 (physical pin 22), which is driven HIGH for 200 ms whenever the measured weight exceeds a threshold of 1000 grams. Implement the HX711 bit-bang read protocol: wait for DOUT to go LOW (data ready), clock out 24 bits MSB-first, then send one additional clock pulse to select Channel A / Gain 128, and convert the 24-bit two's-complement reading to a signed 32-bit integer. Average 5 readings per measurement cycle and compute weight as (average_raw - tare_offset) / scale, performing a startup tare by averaging 10 readings. Check every libgpiod call; if DOUT does not go LOW within 1 second, log an error and retry up to 3 times before exiting. Release all GPIO lines and chips, close syslog, and ensure the solenoid is set LOW on every exit path, handling SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown. Log informational and error messages via syslog. Accept optional command-line arguments --threshold <grams>, --scale <factor>, and --duration <ms>, and poll weight every 500 ms in the main loop.

prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to implement a smart chicken coop lighting system. Control a 12V relay-connected LED strip via GPIO 17 (active-high) based on ambient light read from a BH1750 sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x23. The relay activates at dusk, when lux falls below 50, and deactivates at dawn, when lux exceeds 200, using a hysteresis loop to prevent rapid toggling. Poll the sensor every 5 seconds, waiting at least 180 ms after issuing the One-Time High-Resolution Mode 2 command (0x21) before reading the 2 bytes of lux data, and convert the raw data to lux by dividing by 1.2. Log all sensor readings and relay state changes to chicken_coop_log.txt in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS: Lux = XXX, Relay = ON/OFF'. Implement comprehensive error handling for pigpio initialization, I2C bus communication, and file I/O; if the sensor fails to respond, log the error and safely turn off the relay. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, the relay GPIO, and the log file on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown via SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to control a 5V relay on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11) via a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7); each valid touch toggles the relay state. Initialize pigpio and check for errors, configure GPIO 4 as input and GPIO 17 as output, and implement software debouncing with a 50 ms stabilization delay, toggling only when the sensor reads HIGH both before and after the delay. Wait for the touch sensor to return LOW before allowing the next toggle (edge detection on touch-release). Log every relay state change to the console with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the new state (ON/OFF). Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown by turning the relay OFF, releasing pigpio resources, and printing an exit message. Check the return value of every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite) and report errors to stderr. Use a 10 ms main-loop sleep to reduce CPU usage, and do not include MQTT or networking code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to read flow rate from a YF-S201 water flow sensor on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11), computing liters per minute (LPM) from its 450 pulses-per-liter calibration as LPM = (pulses / 450.0) * 60.0. Trigger a solenoid valve on GPIO 27 to shut off when the rate exceeds 5.0 L/min, reopening only when it drops below 4.5 L/min (0.5 L/min hysteresis); the solenoid is open (HIGH) by default and closes (LOW) above the threshold. Initialize pigpio and validate all return codes (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite, gpioSetISRFuncEx), using a 1-second ISR debounce timeout on the flow sensor pin. Protect the shared pulse counter with a pthread mutex; sample the pulse count every 1 second and reset it after computing LPM. Log every LPM reading and every solenoid state change with timestamps to water_flow.log; if the log file cannot be opened, clean up all initialized resources and exit with a non-zero status. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by logging the event, reopening the solenoid to its safe state, closing the log file, destroying the mutex, and calling gpioTerminate.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library, not bcm2835 or wiringPi, to read data from an HX711 load cell amplifier connected to GPIO 23 (DATA) and GPIO 24 (SCK), calibrate the readings using a known weight, and control an SG90-style servo motor on GPIO 18 via hardware PWM to dispense a pre-determined amount of ingredient based on the weight. The program must act as a TCP server listening on 127.0.0.1:12345: receive a target weight in grams from a client, open the servo to dispense, wait 1 second for the load cell to stabilize, read the actual weight from the HX711, send the actual weight back to the client, and log each dispensing event (date, time, target weight, actual weight, and any error message) as a JSON object appended to dispensing_log.json. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialization, HX711 communication timeouts (sensor absent or not ready), servo control failures, file I/O, and network errors. Use signal handlers (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for clean shutdown of GPIO, sockets, and the servo. Read calibration_factor, server_ip, and server_port from a config.ini file, falling back to defaults if the file is missing or malformed. Read the HX711 using bit-banged GPIO with a 1 µs clock pulse width, timing out if DATA stays HIGH for more than 1000 attempts. Map the target weight to the servo's 1000-2000 µs pulse-width range.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the modern libgpiod API, not wiringPi, to monitor a conveyor-belt motor using an A3144 Hall-effect sensor on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM). A two-pole magnet on the motor shaft produces one pulse per revolution, detected on the rising edge. Configure GPIO 17 as input with the internal pull-up enabled via the GPIOD_LINE_REQUEST_FLAG_BIAS_PULL_UP bias flag, since the A3144's open-collector output requires a pull-up. Use edge-triggered event detection (gpiod_line_event_wait) to count pulses, with a 2 ms debounce window to reject contact bounce and double-edge noise. Every 5 seconds, compute RPM = (pulseCount / 5.0) * 60.0, append the sample to motor_rpm.log in CSV format (timestamp in ISO 8601, rpm_value to 2 decimal places), flushing after every write, and print the current RPM to stdout. Check the return values of gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_chip_get_line, and gpiod_line_request_input_flags, printing clear diagnostics to stderr and exiting non-zero on failure. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop the main loop, release the GPIO line, close the chip, close the log file, and exit cleanly. Use the monotonic clock (clock_gettime with CLOCK_MONOTONIC) for timing, not clock().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to control a 5V relay on GPIO17 based on a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4, which outputs 3.3V logic HIGH when touched and LOW otherwise; the relay module is active-HIGH. On the rising edge of a touch, toggle the relay state, polling the sensor every 50 ms. Implement a failsafe: if the touch sensor remains continuously HIGH for more than 10 seconds, force the relay OFF and ignore further toggles until the sensor is released. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and every gpioSetMode()/gpioWrite()/gpioRead() call; if gpioRead() returns PI_BAD_GPIO, log the error and exit. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a volatile flag so the main loop can exit cleanly; perform the actual cleanup — releasing the relay (set OFF) and calling gpioTerminate() — in main() after the loop exits, not inside the signal handler itself.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to implement a closed-loop flow control system for an ASCO RedHat 8210 series proportional solenoid valve. Drive the valve via PWM on GPIO 18 (BCM, hardware PWM 0), with enable/direction control on GPIO 23 (BCM), active-high, and count pulses from a YF-S201 flow sensor on GPIO 24 (BCM) via an interrupt-driven, rising-edge pulse counter. Accept the target flow rate in L/min as a command-line argument (-t, e.g. -t 5.0), validating it and exiting with an error message if missing or invalid. Sample the flow rate every 100 ms, computing L/min from the pulse count accumulated over the interval using the YF-S201 calibration of 450 pulses per liter, and use a proportional controller (Kp = 1.0) to adjust the valve PWM duty cycle (0-255), clamped to [0, 255], to maintain the target flow rate. Log timestamp_ms, flow_rate, and valve_position to flow_log.csv on every control iteration, logging only to this local file with no UDP or network logging. Enable the valve (GPIO 23 high) at startup; on shutdown, set PWM to 0, drive GPIO 23 low, close the log file, and cleanly terminate pigpio. Check pigpio initialization, GPIO mode setup, ISR registration, and file open, exiting with a diagnostic on any failure, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown and resource release.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to implement a two-factor authentication system controlling two YLI YM-180 electromagnetic lock actuators on GPIO 17 and GPIO 27. The locks are normally engaged (powered = locked); disengage them by driving their GPIO pins LOW for 5 seconds, then re-engage them (HIGH). Authentication requires both factors in sequence: a valid RFID tag read via SPI channel 0 at 100 kHz, where the reader returns 10 bytes and an all-zero response means 'no tag present' rather than an error, matched against the 10-byte valid tag {0x01..0x0A}; then a button press on GPIO 22 (active-low with internal pull-up, 50 ms debounce). On successful two-factor authentication, drive both lock pins LOW for 5 seconds, then re-engage. Log all access attempts — successful, invalid tag, RFID read failure, and button press without a valid tag — with ISO-8601 timestamps to /var/log/door_access.log. Check gpioInitialise(), spiOpen(), spiXfer(), gpioWrite(), and the log file open, handling SPI read failures gracefully without crashing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown: close SPI, release both locks to the engaged state, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate(). Use a non-blocking polling loop with gpioDelay, avoiding busy-wait.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library, not wiringPi, to control two L298N-driven DC motors, implementing a PID controller (KP=1.0, KI=0.1, KD=0.01, 100 ms sample time) to maintain a target rotational speed for each motor, measured by quadrature encoders with 600 pulses per revolution. Motor 1 uses ENA on GPIO 23, IN1 on GPIO 24, IN2 on GPIO 25; Motor 2 uses ENB on GPIO 12, IN3 on GPIO 16, IN4 on GPIO 20. Encoder 1 uses A on GPIO 5, B on GPIO 6; Encoder 2 uses A on GPIO 26, B on GPIO 19. Decode the quadrature signals using libgpiod BOTH_EDGES edge events on each A pin, reading the corresponding B pin to determine direction, and drive each motor with software PWM via libgpiod line toggling at a fixed frequency such as 100 Hz, with duty cycle proportional to the PID output. Target RPMs may be hardcoded, for example 60 RPM for both motors. Log motor speeds (RPM), the PID P/I/D components, and the PID output to motor_log.csv with a header row, flushing after each write. Check all libgpiod calls (chip open, line request, edge event setup) and file operations, and handle encoder read failures gracefully. Use threads for encoder event monitoring so it does not block the main control loop, protecting shared encoder counts with mutexes. Install signal handlers (SIGINT, SIGTERM) that stop the motors, release the GPIO lines, close the chips, and close the log file, and run the control loop indefinitely until interrupted.

I have written a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library, not wiringPi, to control two L298N-driven DC motors, implementing a PID controller (KP=1.0, KI=0.1, KD=0.01, 100 ms sample time) to maintain a target rotational speed for each motor, measured by quadrature encoders with 600 pulses per revolution. Motor 1 uses ENA on GPIO 23, IN1 on GPIO 24, IN2 on GPIO 25; Motor 2 uses ENB on GPIO 12, IN3 on GPIO 16, IN4 on GPIO 20. Encoder 1 uses A on GPIO 5, B on GPIO 6; Encoder 2 uses A on GPIO 26, B on GPIO 19. Decode the quadrature signals using libgpiod BOTH_EDGES edge events on each A pin, reading the corresponding B pin to determine direction, and drive each motor with software PWM via libgpiod line toggling at a fixed frequency such as 100 Hz, with duty cycle proportional to the PID output. Target RPMs may be hardcoded, for example 60 RPM for both motors. Log motor speeds (RPM), the PID P/I/D components, and the PID output to motor_log.csv with a header row, flushing after each write. Check all libgpiod calls (chip open, line request, edge event setup) and file operations, and handle encoder read failures gracefully. Use threads for encoder event monitoring so it does not block the main control loop, protecting shared encoder counts with mutexes. Install signal handlers (SIGINT, SIGTERM) that stop the motors, release the GPIO lines, close the chips, and close the log file, and run the control loop indefinitely until interrupted.

I have written a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library, not wiringPi or pigpio, to control two Adafruit Solenoid Valves (Product ID 997), each a 12V, 0.7A valve switched through a relay module rather than driven directly, implementing a timed water distribution schedule for a miniature automated greenhouse. Valve 1's relay is on GPIO 17 (BCM) and Valve 2's relay is on GPIO 18 (BCM), where GPIO HIGH means the relay is ON and the valve is open, and GPIO LOW means the relay is OFF and the valve is closed. Run the schedule indefinitely until interrupted: activate Valve 1 for 500 ms, then pause 5 seconds; activate Valve 2 for 1000 ms, then pause 10 seconds. Implement robust error handling for GPIO chip initialization failures, gpiod_line_request_output failures, and file I/O errors for logging. Log every valve activation event with an ISO 8601 timestamp to valve_log.txt. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to ensure clean GPIO release and file closure, releasing all GPIO lines and closing the log file on exit.
