prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 upon each successful touch event from an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A (SDA=GPIO2, SCL=GPIO3). Initialize the MPR121 in stop mode, set the touch threshold (0x10) and release threshold (0x0A) for all 12 electrodes, configure the filter/charge time (0x20) and electrode current (0x01), then enter run mode with ELE_EN=1 (0x20) and wait 100 ms for stabilization. Set the relay pin as output, initially off. In a loop with a 100 ms delay, read the touch status registers (0x00-0x01); if any electrode is touched (touch_status > 0), toggle the relay and print the status. Include robust error handling for all I2C operations, GPIO operations, and initialization failures, opening the I2C bus with error handling. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by closing I2C and terminating pigpio.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to detect motion via an HC-SR501 PIR sensor on GPIO 17 (input with pull-down). On a rising-edge motion detection (0 to 1), activate a 5V relay on GPIO 18 (output) for 500 ms to momentarily unlock an electric door strike. Implement rate limiting: ignore subsequent motion events for 2 seconds after each unlock. Log all events — motion detected, door unlocked, and rate-limited events — with millisecond-precision timestamps to door_events.log. Handle pigpio initialization failure gracefully with a clear error message and exit code 1. Ensure proper cleanup on SIGINT or normal exit: close the log file, terminate pigpio, and set the relay off. Use a single thread with non-blocking polling at a 50 ms interval and edge detection, using no sensors or GPIOs beyond the ones specified.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to modulate the speed of two eccentric rotating mass (ERM) vibration motors, Precision Microdrives 310-101, on GPIO pins 17 and 27, generating randomized haptic feedback patterns. Each pattern consists of a sequence of 5 to 15 steps, where each step specifies a PWM duty cycle from 0 to 255 for each motor and a duration of 50-200 ms. Use gpioPWM for PWM control and gpioDelay for timing. Implement robust error handling: check the gpioInitialise return value, verify GPIO mode setting, handle memory allocation failures, and ensure graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by stopping the motors and releasing resources, using a volatile sig_atomic_t shutdown flag. Seed the random number generator with time(NULL), and run indefinitely, generating and playing patterns until interrupted.
raw:
```
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <time.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <pigpio.h>

#define MOTOR1 17
#define MOTOR2 27

volatile sig_atomic_t shutdown = 0;

void sigint_handler(int signum)
{
    shutdown = 1;
}

void init_gpio(void)
{
    if (gpioInitialise() < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "gpioInitialise failed\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    if (gpioSetMode(MOTOR1, PI_OUTPUT) < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "gpioSetMode failed\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    if (gpioSetMode(MOTOR2, PI_OUTPUT) < 0)
    {
        fprintf(stderr, "gpioSetMode failed\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
}

void cleanup_gpio(void)
{
    gpioTerminate();
}

void play_pattern(int motor, int duty, int duration)
{
    gpioPWM(motor, duty);
    usleep(duration * 1000);
}

void play_random_pattern(void)
{
    int motor1_duty = rand() % 256;
    int motor2_duty = rand() % 256;
    int duration = rand() % 150 + 50;

    play_pattern(MOTOR1, motor1_duty, duration);
    play_pattern(MOTOR2, motor2_duty, duration);
}

int main(void)
{
    srand(time(NULL));

    signal(SIGINT, sigint_handler);

    init_gpio();

    while (!shutdown)
    {
        play_random_pattern();
    }

    cleanup_gpio();

    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

The three active-low IR sensors are connected to GPIO4, GPIO17, and GPIO27; the motor driver's PWM inputs are connected to GPIO22, GPIO23, GPIO24, and GPIO25 and run at 1 kHz. Initialize pigpio with error checking, then read all three sensors every 10 ms and apply this control law: if the middle sensor reads low, drive straight at a base speed of 150 out of 255; if only the left sensor reads low, turn right by halving the left motor's speed; if only the right sensor reads low, turn left by halving the right motor's speed; if no sensor reads low, stop both motors. Log each control cycle to trace_log.txt with an ISO 8601 timestamp, the three sensor states as 0 or 1, and the left and right motor speeds. Include robust error handling for pigpio initialization, file opening, and GPIO operations, use only the pigpio API and never wiringPi, and on SIGINT stop the motors, close the log file, terminate pigpio, and release all GPIOs before exiting.

Trigger a relay connected to GPIO23 to activate a grow lamp whenever the lux reading falls below 150. Log every lux reading and every relay state change to grow_log.txt with millisecond-precision timestamps. Handle I2C errors gracefully: if the sensor is not detected or a read fails, log the error and continue without crashing. The program must run indefinitely until SIGINT is received, then cleanly release all resources — close the I2C handle, turn off the relay, and terminate pigpio. Use only C and standard POSIX APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the pigpio library to control a door lock with a servo motor on GPIO18 (PWM-capable) and two push buttons, a lock button on GPIO21 and an unlock button on GPIO22, each using an external or internal pull-up so that pressing reads as active-low (0). When the lock button is pressed, move the servo to the locked position with a pulse width of 1000 microseconds (about 0 degrees); when the unlock button is pressed, move it to the unlocked position with a pulse width of 2000 microseconds (about 180 degrees). Debounce each button press with a 100 ms delay. Constrain the servo pulse width to the safe range of 500-2500 microseconds at all times. Handle initialization failures gracefully, print status messages, use only pigpio API calls and never wiringPi, and cleanly release all resources on exit through a SIGINT signal handler.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads ambient light levels from four BH1750FVI sensors on the I2C-1 bus at 7-bit addresses 0x23, 0x24, 0x25, and 0x26, using the standard Linux I2C ioctl interface (<linux/i2c-dev.h> with open() and ioctl(I2C_SLAVE)) rather than wiringPi. Note that the BH1750 natively supports only addresses 0x23 and 0x5C via its ADDR pin, so addresses 0x24-0x26 require an I2C multiplexer or level-shifted address lines; assume the hardware is wired accordingly. For each sensor, open /dev/i2c-1 (a single shared file descriptor or one per sensor is acceptable), set the slave address with ioctl(I2C_SLAVE, addr) before each transaction, write the One-Time High-Resolution mode command byte 0x20, wait 180 ms for conversion, then read 2 bytes. Convert the big-endian result to lux using lux = ((data[0] << 8) | data[1]) / 1.2. Once per second, broadcast all four readings as a single UDP multicast packet to 239.255.255.250:5005, formatted as semicolon-separated sensor_id,lux pairs, e.g. 1,120.5;2,85.0;3,210.5;4,45.0. If any sensor fails — open error, address-set error, write error, read error, or partial read — report NaN for that sensor and continue. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by setting a flag to exit the loop cleanly, and close all file descriptors, both I2C and UDP socket, on every exit path.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads airflow data from a Honeywell AWM7300V mass airflow sensor at I2C address 0x28 on /dev/i2c-1, using the Linux I2C character device interface (<linux/i2c-dev.h>, <sys/ioctl.h>, read() and write() syscalls) rather than wiringPi. To read flow data, issue a zero-length I2C write as a start condition followed by a 2-byte read; the sensor returns a 14-bit flow value in the first two bytes, masked with 0x3FFF. Convert the raw value to SLPM using flow = (raw - 3277) * 0.1, sampling once per second, and log each timestamped flow rate to airflow_log.txt. Check every syscall, retry transient I2C read failures up to 3 times with 100 ms delays between retries, and handle sensor-absent (ENXIO) and bus-error (EIO) conditions. Install a SIGINT handler that closes the I2C file descriptor and flushes the log file for a clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an Adafruit AS7341 10-Channel Light/Color Sensor over I2C using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface — opening /dev/i2c-1 and using ioctl with I2C_SLAVE to set the 7-bit address 0x39 — rather than wiringPi. Perform a proper initialization sequence: verify the WHO_AM_I/ID register at 0x24 equals 0x19, power the sensor on via the PON bit in the ENABLE register at 0x80, configure SMUX for spectral readings via the CFG6 register at 0xAF, and enable spectral measurement via the SP_EN bit. Read all 10 spectral channels — F1 through F8, Clear, and NIR — from their registers at 0x60-0x73, compute a simplified lux approximation, and log the results with a timestamp to spectral_log.csv every 5 seconds in comma-separated format. Check every I2C read and write return value, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release, closing both the I2C file descriptor and the log file, on all exit paths including SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with an Omron D7S seismic sensor over I2C using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (opening /dev/i2c-1 and using ioctl I2C_SLAVE) rather than wiringPi. The sensor's default 7-bit I2C address is 0x37. Read the 6 bytes of tri-axial acceleration starting at register 0x28 — X_L, X_H, Y_L, Y_H, Z_L, Z_H, little-endian signed 16-bit — and convert to g using g = raw * 0.000244 for the ±8 g range. At 1-second intervals by default, log timestamped X, Y, Z values in g to seismic_data.csv with columns timestamp,x_g,y_g,z_g. Check every I2C read and write return value, retry transient failures up to 3 times with a 10 ms backoff, detect sensor-absent and bus-error conditions, and log all errors with timestamps to seismic_error.log. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C file descriptor and flushing and closing the CSV file on all exit paths. Support command-line options -a for the I2C address (default 0x37), -i for the interval in seconds (default 1), and -f for the output filename (default seismic_data.csv).

Initialize the sensor by sending the power-on command 0x01 followed by the continuous high-resolution mode command 0x10. Every 1 second, read the 16-bit big-endian raw value, convert it to lux using lux = raw / 1.2, and broadcast the value as a floating-point string over UDP multicast to 239.255.255.250:5000 with TTL set to 1. Check every I2C write and read operation for failure, and on sensor absence or a bus error, print an error and retry after 1 second. Use a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM to properly clean up the I2C file descriptor and socket on exit, and run indefinitely using standard POSIX sockets until interrupted.
